speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's prohibition
against the importation of swine, uncooked pork and uncooked pork products from the United States is being removed as of this date. The embargo was imposed in 1952 under the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, following a severe outbreak of vesicular exanthema in the United States.
The United States declared its swine industry free of vesicular exanthema on October 22 last year, and there has been no actual outbreak of the disease since November, 1956. Discussions between veterinary officials of the two countries satisfied Canadian authorities that the disease no longer poses a threat to the Canadian swine industry.
The removal of the restrictions on United States pork imports into Canada now that vesicular exanthema has been eradicated in the United States, is in keeping with the principle followed in dealing with international restrictions on animal health grounds. The embargo imposed by the United States against the import of Canadian meats, after the outbreak of foot and mouth disease in Canada in 1952, was removed following certification by Canadian veterinary authorities that the disease had been eradicated.
More recently, in 1959, certain states had imposed embargoes against Canadian sheep because Canadian measures for the control of scrapie disease were not considered as rigid as those followed in the United States. The Canadian control program was revised to make it equivalent to that of the United States, and the state embargoes have since been withdrawn.

maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING
subtopic: MOTION TO STANDARDIZE BEGINNING AND ENDING
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this house the government should initiate a policy of standardizing the dates of beginning and terminating daylight saving time in the six time zones of this country.
He said: Down through the years the people of Canada have used different systems of

time, beginning with solar time. Following that, on the advice of Sir Sandford Fleming the country adopted the present system. Slightly less than half a century ago Sir Robert Borden, as a war measure introduced provision for daylight saving time. We know this was meant strictly as a wartime measure and we know, of course, that it was used during the second world war for the same purpose at the instance of the federal level of government. Since those years it has been generally accepted as a standard of time throughout the country.
It is difficult to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this system as it affects the entire country, but it is not the intention of my motion to promote such a discussion. And in speaking of the motion itself I may say it would be a simple matter to take a somewhat negative attitude with regard to it. It could be said, as indeed it has been, that it is unconstitutional, or matters could be left strictly as they are and thus remain in a disorganized state of confusion.
I hasten to admit that I have made one slight error, in stating that there are six time zones across the country. In actual fact there are seven; Newfoundland, Atlantic, eastern, central, mountain, Pacific and Yukon times.
I have discussed this matter with a learned constitutional authority, and have been advised that this matter may be legally discussed and dealt with at this level of government. However, in the motion itself I have used the word "initiate" which will eliminate the possibility of any embarrassment in the event that I have been mislead by my counsel. This will also serve to eliminate the possibility of embarrassment resulting from any action taken by this house or by the government in this regard. This would leave it open to this level of government to participate in discussions arising from this motion and any action resulting therefrom.
In reviewing the question of daylight saving time in Canada at the present time I note that it is controlled in four provinces. In one of these it is outlawed, while in the remaining provinces it is left to the discretion of the local government to determine its applicability. I do not have to remind the house or the government of the keen interest taken in this matter by the smaller towns and rural areas. Since members of municipal government have not the time to investigate annually the decisions of towns in their areas, it seems to me that the federal government could give valuable leadership in this matter as it has done so capably in other fields.

The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities has petitioned the government sufficiently on this matter to warrant this consideration and perhaps to lead it to institute action. In a pamphlet entitled "A National Municipal Program" the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities clearly states that the federation may represent the public interest at the national level in matters which are generally the responsibility of municipal government.
I should like to place on the record the most recent resolution on this subject proposed by the national federation of mayors and municipalities at its conference in 1958:
Whereas the adoption of daylight saving time each year by various municipalities across Canada, while other communities remain on standard time, causes great confusion throughout the whole country; and whereas the country-wide uniformity as to time and regulations would eliminate such confusion;
Therefore, be it resolved that the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities request the dominion and provincial authorities to consider recommending the necessary legislation in order to bring about uniformity in daylight saving time regulations throughout the whole country.
It could be argued on this point that the words of that resolution are at considerable variance with the words of the motion. However, the intent is very similar, and in my opinion the achievement of uniformity in this regard would assist the Canadian economy in general.
It is a well known fact that any leadership in the establishment of uniformity has come about on the part of the railway association of Canada, which has a vital interest in the matter. Although there are many other facets of Canadian life to which this matter is equally vital, particularly business life and probably thousands of personal issues, I feel that a much greater degree of uniformity and satisfaction could be achieved were this matter to be dealt with by the federal government.
As I indicated, to a large degree the railway association governs the dates of commencement and termination of our system of daylight saving time after a general canvass of the larger cities and towns of the country. This, of course, is the way it must be on account of. the economic conditions in those larger centres, but there are smaller towns which have substantial industries and which are, in my opinion, discriminated against because of the lack of uniformity. Consequently in many instances there is a substantial business loss. It is not my intention to cause any discussion or any undue argument, as between urban and rural areas, but if we are realistic it is not difficult to realize that this system of daylight saving time has
Daylight Saving Time been in existence for a considerable period of time and will continue to be in existence for a further considerable period of time.
I have noted, Mr. Speaker, that the government at Westminster is considering the establishment of double daylight saving time. If adopted this will have to be established, of course, by the central government. I hasten to add that I do not propose to discuss the merits of this or any other system that is observed. I mention it because it will be controlled by the federal government of Great Britain. Further, in my efforts to learn how daylight saving time is administered in other countries I have found that it is controlled by the federal governments of 21 other countries, and possibly more, though this information was not available to me when I investigated this particular point.
It is not difficult to realize the serious situation in regard to the towns and villages to which I have made reference. I can assure the house that I am aware of several instances where there are from five to eight municipalities within a radius of from 15 to 20 miles, each of which terminates its observance of daylight saving time on a different date extending anywhere from Labour day week end to the last week end of October. Hon. members will realize immediately that this can be very important and costly, particularly with respect to transportation services, broadcasting schedules, business life and so on. I am thinking now particularly of the many commuters who go from town to town to earn their living.
As I mentioned, it is not only inconvenient but very costly. I feel that the answer to the problem as I have outlined it may very well lie within the terms of the resolution I have presented. This resolution if adopted would cause the cities, towns and villages, or anyone wishing to observe daylight saving time, to begin and terminate such observance on the same day. I would emphasize to the house that there is no compulsion in the terms of the resolution, that is for the observance of daylight saving time. There is no compulsion at all in the resolution, so it should have no bearing on the arguments that have been raised in the past, or likely to be raised in the future, by people in the rural areas. The regulation is simply aimed at uniformity, as I have stressed.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I have proposed this resolution. If there are other hon. members who wish to voice their views on this particular matter I am certainly prepared to hear and consider those views. I should like also to assure the house that as a result of the inquiries I have made amongst

Daylight Saving Time
the members I have found quite a measure of agreement, because certainly the people who live in the larger centres are in agreement and the other centres would merely incorporate this system in their plans.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in an effort to curtail lengthy and useless debate, I would suggest that after other hon. members have voiced their sentiments we get the concurrence of the house in the motion.

maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING
subtopic: MOTION TO STANDARDIZE BEGINNING AND ENDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with due respect to the hon. member who sponsored this resolution, who hails from an eastern Ontario county and who may have some justification for advocating daylight saving in his own region, I must say that I could not agree with him that the government should initiate a policy of standardizing daylight saving time in all parts of Canada. The lakehead region does not need and does not want daylight saving, for the simple reason that the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur, and the district, are on eastern standard time. It could be said that we are in fact on daylight saving all the year round, by virtue of the fact that we are a thousand miles west of the region of the hon. member who moved this resolution.
In the district of Thunder Bay we are exactly one hour ahead of Toronto and Ottawa by sun time. The city councils and chambers of commerce of the twin cities have repeatedly gone on record against any proposal for the adoption of daylight saving. In 1941 daylight saving was made compulsory throughout Canada as a war measure and the two cities, though reluctantly, went along with it.
Our experience on that occasion was not good. We did not like it because during the months of May and June the sun did not set until 10 or 11 p.m., and it had the effect of keeping the school children up late. They simply would not go to bed while the sun was still up. Our farmers did not like it because it upset the milking routine of their cows, and I daresay even the cows did not like it. The only people who relished the extra hour of daylight were the golfers and the baseball fans. Now we have floodlighted playgrounds for baseball so, even in that regard there is no longer the necessity to provide extra daylight.
If any region wishes to implement daylight saving for the benefit of its communities, such as those in the constituency of the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler), all well and good. I would be the last to object to such a proposal; but to try to force daylight saving on districts where instead of a blessing it would be an unwanted menace, does not appear to me to be sound legislation.

The only justification for such a measure would be the production of beneficial results to the people concerned. So far as I know, no benefits could possibly be expected from the introduction of daylight saving time in places such as the lakehead, where we already are one hour ahead, by sun time, by comparison with most regions in Canada.
I submit that this resolution if adopted would mean blanket approval of a measure of doubtful value, and one which would represent an invasion of the right of people in various regions to determine for themselves whether or not they approve of daylight saving. The request for such a measure should come from the communities desirous of such legislation. I do not see how the hon. member for Grey-Bruce can reconcile his suggestion that all regions would not be obliged to follow this legislation. If such legislation were passed then, so far as I am concerned, this would be a policy for the whole of Canada to observe.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) brought the matter of daylight saving time to the attention of the house a couple of years ago. At that time his suggestion, if I remember correctly, was that the question should be referred to a federal-provincial conference. It seems to me that this is, after all, a question which comes under provincial jurisdiction. The provinces would be more conversant with the wishes of the people in the various sections of their domain.
I sincerely trust that this resolution, notwithstanding the good intentions of the mover -and I have every sympathy with him- will not pass this house. In other words, so far as I am concerned I will vote against it, and I would urge every member to do the same, especially if they live in regions, as I do, where the sun does not set for an hour after many people in Ottawa and Toronto have gone to bed.

maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING
subtopic: MOTION TO STANDARDIZE BEGINNING AND ENDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to be even briefer today than I normally am. I should like hon. members to pay close attention to the wording of this resolution. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should initiate a policy of standardizing the dates of beginning and terminating daylight saving time in the six time zones of this country.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is a policy that could be supported by every hon. member in this house. The people in this country who are interested in the problem of daylight saving time are divided into two groups, those who think it is a good thing and those who think it is a bad thing. Surely those who believe it is a good thing must agree that if we are going to have a good thing

it should start on the same day all across the country and finish on the same day. In so far as those who think it is a bad thing are concerned, then I say it is a good thing to have a bad thing start on the same day and finish on the same day all across the country.
I would suggest, therefore, in view of the fact that there have been some rumblings both inside and outside this house to the effect that we have tended, on occasion, to waste a little time, that this is one occasion when we can save time by passing this resolution and getting on with something else.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex Wesl):
maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING
subtopic: MOTION TO STANDARDIZE BEGINNING AND ENDING
speechtext:
should like to make just a few brief remarks on this resolution. The use of daylight saving time is a matter of great concern to both the urban and rural people in the part of the country which I have the honour to represent, Middlesex West.
Generally speaking the urban people are strongly in favour of the use of daylight saving time during the summer months. By moving the working hours of the day ahead, a longer after-work period is established. That period can be used for working around the home, gardening or recreation. On the other hand the rural people or, at any rate, a great many of them are strongly opposed to the use of daylight saving time. It upsets their schedules for milking cows and doing the other farm work, work which is largely governed by sun time which is the nearest thing we can get to standard time.
In order to indicate the feeling of some of these people may I say that a short time ago I received a resolution from the Napier women's institute, which is a fine body of women in our constituency. I believe all hon. members of this house are familiar with the work of women's institutes in Canada. If not, I would say they are a national body organized to promote better living conditions in the rural areas of our country. The resolution covers a number of points of which I think the house should be aware when it is considering this matter. The resolution of the women's institute reads as follows:
Whereas our organization works for the best interests in our home and our country; and
whereas daylight saving time is causing ill feeling between rural and urban people and is increasing the tension of modern living in our homes; and
whereas it is upsetting to the health and habits of our children and teen-agers; and
whereas making adjustments to the new time is not conducive to early retiring or attention to studies because of prolonged daylight and is a drawback on fall mornings especially to rural school children; and
whereas it in no way increases productive power but has worked hardship on the farmer since a considerable amount of his work is governed by sun time; and
Daylight Saving Time
whereas hired help insist on working by the clock; and
whereas it has caused confusion in transportation circles where new schedules have had to be drawn to fit in with new times; and
whereas starting and ending daylight saving time dates have varied in different counties and added to the confusion;
Therefore be it resolved that our government through this resolution bring about the final abolition of daylight saving time.
The president of the association is Mrs. John A. McNeil and the secretary is Mrs. Wilbert Dinning. The resolution was moved by Mrs. John Clothier and seconded by Mrs. Bruce Hay.
In that resolution there are one or two points that might stand further elaboration. One is that which has to do with the setting up of transportation schedules. As hon. members know, high school children and a great many elementary school children go to school in buses. In that area a condition has arisen under which different times are being used in adjacent municipalities, and it becomes an extremely confusing matter to prepare bus schedules for the transportation of the school children. Of all the reasons why daylight saving time causes irritation to rural people, I think this one matter of the difficulty of setting up schedules for school buses is the most outstanding.
There is another matter touched on in this resolution, wherein it states that hired help insist on working by the clock. Much of a farmer's work must be done in those hours when conditions are right. This statement applies to haying, harvesting and certain other matters. When the hours of work for hired help are fixed on the basis of standard time, any change causes irritation between the hired help and the farm employer. For these various reasons the rural people are strongly opposed to the use of daylight saving time. They would prefer to remain on standard time.
As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce in moving this resolution, the federal parliament of Canada has little jurisdiction over the setting of time zones, etc. He pointed out that we have seven different time zones in Canada. We could go into quite a long discussion on the reason for these zones, but I think we can spend our time to better advantage by getting right down to the authority which is responsible for setting the time in the municipalities.
I understand that about two years ago the province of Saskatchewan made the use of daylight saving time general all over that province but that, because they found so much dissatisfaction over the matter, the legislation was repealed in the following

Daylight Saving Time year. The province of Alberta have decided not to use daylight saving time in that province, though the municipalities on their own initiative may use it if they so desire.
I am going to quote briefly from chapter 90 of the revised statutes of Ontario, 1950, the definition of time act. It is a very short act and, as far as we in Ontario are concerned, it quite clearly outlines who has the authority to deal with this problem of daylight saving time in Ontario. Section 1 of the definition of time act reads as follows:
1. (1) Where an expression of time occurs in any act or in any rule of court, bylaw, deed or other instrument, heretofore or hereafter enacted or executed, or where any hour or other period of time is stated either orally or in writing, or any question as to a period of time arises, the time referred to or intended shall, unless it is otherwise specifically stated, be held to be "standard time".
(2)	As regards that part of Ontario which lies east of the meridian of ninety degrees west longitude, standard time shall be reckoned as five hours behind Greenwich time.
(3)	As regards that part of Ontario which lies west of that meridian, standard time shall be reckoned as six hours behind Greenwich time.
(4)	The lieutenant governor in council may from time to time make regulations, and may from time to time amend, modify, suspend, repeal and re-enact such regulations, varying the reckoning of standard time as defined by subsections 2 and 3.
(5)	Such regulations may authorize the Ontario municipal board to fix the timetables of all railways subject to its control, and to make such other orders as may be necessary for the convenient carrying out of the provisions of this act, in so far as may be necessary or convenient for carrying out the regulations.
Section 2 reads:
The expression "month", where it occurs or is stated as in section 1 mentioned, means a calendar month unless it is otherwise specifically stated.
Section 3 reads:
The hours of the day may in any locality be numbered in one series up to twenty four.
That is the whole of the definition of the time act as it appears in chapter 90 of the revised statutes of Ontario, 1950. Section 260 of the municipal act being chapter 243 of the revised statutes of Ontario, 1950 reads as follows:
Every council may pass such bylaws and make such regulations for the health, safety, morality and welfare of the inhabitants of the municipality in matters not specifically provided for by this act, as may be deemed expedient and are not contrary to law, and for governing the proceedings of the council, the conduct of its members and the calling of meetings.
This indicates that the matter of time could come under the authority of section 260 of the municipal act of Ontario.
I do not wish to take up more time, Mr. Speaker. There is no unanimity on this matter of using daylight saving time. There was a time when the majority of the population of Canada lived on the farms. That time

has gone. Now there are only about 12 per cent to 15 per cent of the working force of Canada employed on the farms of this country. Or course the people so employed will have to fit in as best they can if a preponderance of public opinion favours the use of daylight saving time. In our own area of southwestern Ontario there is much to be said for it and there is much to be said against it.
I believe this resolution is a good resolution, and is the best we can do in view of the fact that there are such strong and sharp differences of opinion concerning the use of daylight saving time. At least to make it uniform in certain areas would help to cut down some of the confusion caused by it.

I have made this suggestion over a period of years on the estimates of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois), and I must say that I am flattered to know that my ideas have had some effect upon Progressive Conservative members' thinking. That frequently occurs from this end of the house. If you read back in Hansard over the years you will find where we have advocated something; then finally it has begun to seep into the consciousness of our friends opposite; then someone is brave enough to advance it before the house, and some years later it may even become legislation.

speechtext:
I will agree, Mr. Speaker, that we are always subject to influence, but I am glad to say that in this group we are subject very slightly to bad influence.
When we are discussing this question it must be realized it is not a question of whether or not we like daylight saving time. I sympathize with the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) and the cows he was speaking for. Daylight saving, in effect, is almost general in Canada. That is what we have to realize. I know the attitude of farm people, and so on, but in my opinion it is about time we ended this ludicrous, self-imposed inconvenience. In my own district we have mountain time, Pacific time, standard time and daylight saving time, and you can imagine the confusion and unnecessary inconvenience caused in meeting buses or trains. Our trains run on standard time, our buses run partly on mountain time and partly on Pacific time, and so on. I think we should face the fact that generally speaking national time is the wish of the majority of Canadians

at this time, and we should do something to get agreement on what, in my opinion, is a very simple matter in view of all the circumstances.
I support the hon. member's resolution, in principle and in spirit, because he is trying to get federal government to initiate his proposal. This does not mean that the federal government will impose its will on the provinces. I think the federal government, under the direction and guidance of the genial Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys-who I am pleased to note, Mr. Speaker, visited my constituency last summer and had a most delightful picture of himself taken and placed in the papers-should initiate discussions on this matter, I suggest at a federal-provincial conference.
I did not intend, in speaking on this question over the years, to indicate that such a conference would be a large affair costing very much money; it is simply a question of a representative from each province meeting with representatives of the federal government, sitting down and dealing with the situation as it exists, and then coming to an agreement that this, as I said before, ludicrous, self-imposed inconvenience should end.
I think there is general support for this policy across Canada, perhaps with the exception of a few isolated and backwoods communities. I think all that is necessary is an application of common sense, with a spirit of co-operation, to remedy what to me seems a silly and unnecessary situation in this day and generation.
That is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on this motion, I must say that in principle I do support legislation of some kind to provide a uniform system of daylight saving time across Canada, thereby eliminating the confusion existing today by having some municipalities on daylight saving and some not.
Daylight saving has been in force in many parts of Canada for many years. This indicates quite clearly that it has the support of many Canadians. However, I always feel that as members of this house we should not be too ready to put into legislative form ideas or opinions of our own without first being satisfied that we are doing what we believe to be the wish of the majority of our people.
Therefore, in order to give us a chance to study this motion more carefully, and on the understanding that we will have an opportunity to consider the matter further at some future time, I move that the debate be now adjourned.

This resolution is couched in broad general terms for two reasons. The first reason is, of course, to enlarge the scope of its appeal so as to solicit the widest possible support. The second is to endeavour to have the debate confined as much as possible to the principle of the resolution. The essential factors in this motion are embodied in phrases which employ words of a relative character. Were more precise language used we might get into a debate on secondary issues. For example, we might become involved in a discussion of what is a small business, or what is meant by a long term loan, or what constitutes low interest rates. It is obvious that interest rates which might be considered low today would have been considered high a few years ago.
It is, of course, evident that if this resolution is ever implemented it will be necessary to bring forward legislation. When that legislation is presented, that will be the time to define these factors in specific terms. Certainly a small business will have to be defined, but the definition will have to be sufficiently flexible to cover different types of enterprises and different types of situations. The criteria will have to vary for different types of businesses; but whichever criteria are used, whether the number of employees or the volume of the turnover, or a combination of both, it will be impossible to escape borderline cases. However, before this legislation can be drawn up it is necessary to debate the principle of providing long term low interest loans to small businessmen, to establish the need for such loans and to solicit ideas as to the best means of attaining this objective and as to the scope of the legislation required. By affording us an opportunity to pool and clarify our ideas on this subject this debate can serve a very useful purpose.
As far as the principle of the resolution is concerned, it is simply an extension of the

Low Interest Loans to Small Business principle already recognized and incorporated in legislation governing the farm loan board, the fisheries loan board, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the industrial development bank. I think we would all agree that the backbone of our economy is not the big corporations but the vast number of independent small enterprises, many of which are family enterprises; that the security and well being of our nation demands that these small businesses be encouraged, and that their actual and potential capacity be developed to the maximum.
The nature of most of our provincial economies is such that they do not lend themselves to the operations of large companies but, rather, to small enterprises serving local needs. This is particularly true in the Atlantic provinces and I believe in the prairie provinces as well. The greater the number of small and prosperous enterprises, the sounder will be our national economy. A community which has 50 small industries each employing 20 persons has a far more stable economy than a community dependent on a single industry employing 1,000 people. Not only is the small operator better able to adapt to changing conditions, but he is also much closer to his employees. Moreover, the more small enterprises there are, the more opportunities we have of developing leadership, initiative and independence; qualities of character which are great national assets.
Unfortunately, however, the law of the jungle too often prevails in the business world. The large devour the small. All too often in the Atlantic provinces we have seen big corporations buy up local businesses and then close them down, or else undercut them until they are forced out of existence. The small businessman is in a particularly difficult position in times of tight money, when he has very little means of protecting himself against the unfair position into which he is forced through no fault of his own.
On the other hand, in times of tight money the big corporations can fall back on alternative sources of financing; often they can get credit from the chartered banks or, if not, they can fall back on the flotation of bond issues. The small businessman cannot do this because the size of his loan is too small to interest the investment houses.
If the little fellow is to survive, some source of long term low interest credit must be made available to him. The industrial development bank is meeting only a small part of this need, since its loans are restricted primarily to manufacturing industries. The majority of our small businesses-our retail stores, drug stores and service industries-do


not qualify for loans from the industrial development bank because they are not primarily manufacturing concerns.
It may be argued that it is the function of the chartered banks to look after the financial needs of this type of small enterprise, but the chartered banks are not meeting this need either, on anything near the scale required. In times of tight money most chartered banks refuse to grant credit on the scale required by the small operator. Even when the small businessman does secure a loan from a chartered bank it is not very satisfactory, because usually it is a very short term loan and payable on demand. This demand hangs over the head of the small businessman like the sword of Damocles, and for that reason many operators who might be able to get short term loans from chartered banks are reluctant to take them for the purpose of expansion and improvement, for fear that the banks may demand repayment of the loans and thus cripple the small operators or put them out of business.
At very best a loan payable on demand requires all the profits of the business for the next three, four or five years, as the case may be, to retire the loan. In a case where the owner has died and left income payable out of profits to his widow and minor children, then the son or sons or whoever is managing the business would be afraid to take a short term loan from a chartered bank because if they were forced to repay it there would be no income to pay the widow and the minor dependents.
To develop their actual and potential capacity to the fullest degree it is essential that small businesses plan an orderly program of expansion and improvement over a period of years, as is done by big corporations such as the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Aluminum Company of Canada. To do this they must be provided with capital advances that can be budgeted for and repaid' in orderly instalments over the lifetime of the improvements.
When it comes to considering the means by which this can be best accomplished, one naturally would wish to explore the possibility of using agencies already in existence. The one that comes first to mind is the industrial development bank. However, even if the scope of the industrial development bank were extended to include other types of small businesses it is doubtful if this would be a suitable agency. Even in its own restricted field the industrial development bank, in my opinion, is not operating in the best interests of the economy as a whole.
The 1959 report of the industrial development bank indicates that only 14 loans have

been made to the province of Newfoundland since confederation in 1949. In the 15 years of its existence the industrial development bank has made loans to 2,866 businesses. Of this figure 1,718 or 60 per cent of the total were made to businesses in Ontario and Quebec. Only 239 or 8 per cent of these loans went to business in the Atlantic provinces, and only 275 or 10 per cent to firms in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
Last year, 1959, was a year of tight money. The total loans made by the industrial development bank in 1959 amounted to $30,579,000. Of that sum $17,447,000 or 59 per cent went to firms in Ontario and Quebec. Only $2.5 million or 8 per cent of the total went to the Atlantic provinces and $3,043,000 or roughly 10 per cent went to the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Thus we see that in a year of tight money 82 per cent of the loans made by the industrial development bank went to areas where inflationary pressures were already high and where unemployment was low, but only 18 per cent went to regions where unemployment was extremely high and where there were no inflationary pressures at all.
Actually, in a time of tight money, in my opinion it should be the other way round. The industrial development bank or a similar agency should act as a balance wheel to inject flexibility into our economy and make money available to those areas where development can take place without increasing the inflationary pressure on the economy as a whole.

speechtext:
I said, Mr. Speaker, I did not consider that the industrial development bank, with its small number of branches dispersed across Canada, would be a suitable agency, even if its scope were enlarged, to give this service. Also, our experience with loans to fishermen indicates that the chartered banks would not be very anxious to enter this field, and even if they did they would not function very satisfactorily. In my opinion what is required is the creation of a new special agency along the lines of that which exists now in the United States, with branches

Low Interest Loans to Small Business widely dispersed throughout Canada after the pattern of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Such an agency could take over the function of the industrial development bank, which could then be abolished. It might also be possible for this new agency to administer loans to farmers and fishermen; it might also be possible to combine it with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the administration of building loans.
The operative word of this resolution is "consideration"; that the government should give urgent consideration to the provision of some means of providing long term low interest loans. No doubt the government has already given consideration to this matter. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has already shown that he is aware of this problem. During the 1957 election he was quoted by the Montreal Star of May 9, 1957 as saying:
This is a country of small business. Of the 37,400 manufacturing establishments in Canada 35,110 employ 99 persons or less. Of these, some 17,000 have fewer than five employees.
There are 150,000 separate retailers in Canada, and 143,000 are independent-These small businesses are the backbone of industry.
The quotation goes on:
The Conservative leader said these concerns were not getting a fair share of government contracts. Nor were they receiving the technical assistance or special consideration in government financial policy which they needed to be able to compete with big business.
A Conservative government would set up a committee of cabinet ministers, small business representatives, economists and other experts to develop a policy favouring establishment of new businesses and expansion of existing small businesses, he declared.
On May 18 the Prime Minister is quoted in the Calgary Herald as having said:
The tight money policy has dealt "a mortal blow" to small industries, and a Conservative government would enact legislation similar to that in the United States which would assist small business.
During the 1958 election the Prime Minister was quoted in the Charlottetown Guardian of February 28, 1958, as saying:
He announced that if his government is re-elected, it is their intention at the first session of parliament to give consideration to a system whereby small business may be able to expand on reasonable terms, and have available to it a system of financing which is being considered to enable small business to meet its responsibility in expanding and assuring extra jobs. A community will continue to prosper and expand if small business expands, he said.
There is no doubt about the need for such legislation, and it is important to the well-being and security of our national economy that this legislation be brought down as quickly as possible.

In view, then, of the personal interest of the Prime Minister in this matter, may we hope that consideration will give way to positive action at a very early date.

maintopic: PROVISION OF LOW INTEREST LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with certain qualifications, which I will mention later, I will state now that I agree with the motion placed before the house. I believe we all agree that in principle the government has no business in the field of lending money. That is a job for lending institutions and banks. When the government lends money, either directly or indirectly by loans or by guaranteeing loans, it is using the funds of some of its citizens to lend to others. Therefore, before loans of any nature of public funds can be justified we have to ask ourselves whether the particular loan meets with the wishes of our people and whether it is in the national interest. However, over the years we have found governments entering the field of direct and indirect loans to different classes of persons throughout the country.
I should like to look for a few minutes at the situation under which this parliament has authorized loans to be made, and try to find out the underlying basis for each type of loan. Undoubtedly the greatest use of public funds for loans in the last two and one half years has been in connection with housing. We have authorized the expenditure of $1 billion of public funds for loans under the National Housing Act, and at the present time we are being asked for a further sum of $500 million. Make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker; in my humble opinion the greatest single factor in maintaining the economy in a stable position in the past two years has been the housing loans. This has been done at a time when a recession of serious proportions seemed imminent and, in my opinion, the program undertaken by the government and authorized by parliament has had the effect which it was intended to bring about.
Now, I think we must examine how we justify such a loan from public funds. First, it should meet a social need of the people for decent houses to live in; second, it should provide markets for national products. Third, it should provide work when work is needed. Fourth, it should give a boost generally to our economy when such a boost is needed. In my opinion, in all particulars, the objectives have been met.
There is another type of loan from public funds which has been popular, and that is agricultural support prices and deficiency payments. The basic reason, I believe, that these loans are authorized is to maintain in a stable position a national occupation which it is desirable to maintain.

We have had a further type of loan, advances for home-stored grain in a previous year, and this year guaranteed bank loans for grain producers to meet temporary difficulties arising from their inability to thresh their grain. In this particular case the basic reason, as I see it, was to meet an emergency situation in a business from which this country derives a tremendous amount of foreign dollars.
Another means we have used to make loans, as has already been mentioned by other hon. members, is through the industrial development bank. I do not intend to enlarge on the comments made. We know that, here again, the bank was set up to assist and encourage the development of manufacturing industries in Canada which was considered a matter of national importance and one which affected the whole country. So, we could go through the list of situations in which public funds have been lent to different classes of people.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, they break down into a number of causes which I should like to enumerate. I feel that wherever public funds are being lent to people in various parts of the country, the following situations should exist: First there should be an urgent or emergency situation, overriding the general rule about loans, which is one of national interest; second, I feel that loans must be made to groups to whom the government, speaking as a whole, has an obligation. Third, I feel that such loans should be a substitute for the government directly entering a particular field. Finally, there should be an inability of lending institutions to meet the situation.
I should like now to apply these tests to the resolution which we have under consideration. It relates to small businesses. I do not intend, as did the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) who introduced the resolution, to attempt to define small business, to define what low interest rates are, and so forth. I accept his invitation to speak in general terms on the resolution in connection with small business. There are cases where there is not an emergency situation which the government has met by other means than direct or indirect loans. There are two matters which the government has undertaken which, in my opinion, indicated the intent of the government to help small businesses. I come back, to the housing program which stimulated small businesses by creating a better atmosphere in this country. This program created opportunities for sales by a lot of small businesses which were directly or indirectly connected with housing. This is one feature of Canadian life which runs all across the country. Indeed, this program gave all types of small business a boost and gave them
Low Interest Loans to Small Business what I feel was a better opportunity than direct loans because it created an atmosphere where loans, in a good many cases, were not required.
This program created what is of greater advantage, an atmosphere in which small business could prosper. As I mentioned, this program was adopted at a time when the profits of a good many small businesses seemed to be dwindling. These housing loans, of course, directly affected the lumbering and building trades, but they were also of concern to a good many workers who are not directly connected with these industries. They also benefited all those with whom small business people dealt.

speechtext: All?

speechtext:
I submit, yes; they did affect indirectly all of those with whom small business people dealt.
There is a section that concerns small business which was set up in the Department of Trade and Commerce in September, 1958. This was another effort to create an atmosphere of prosperity for the small businessmen rather than come to their direct aid with loans. Now, the job of this small business section was to improve opportunities for small businesses in Canada. Frankly, we have not heard too much about the work of this section. I have made some inquiries and I find that they are, in fact, doing a tremendous amount of work to which little publicity has been given. They seem to be carrying out the job for which they were set up.
We talked about this subject on July 16 last. At that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) indicated the reasons which prompted the setting up of the small business section, and he indicated what its job would be. As I say, he reported to parliament on July 16 last, and I am hoping that he will report again at this session concerning the progress made.
The minister indicated that the terms of reference for the small business section were to act as a clearing house in referring inquiries of small businesses to the appropriate department of the Canadian government or provincial and municipal governments or various other organizations; second to compile and distribute bulletins and reports on topics of general interest to small businesses, including information on government procurement; third, to assist small businesses on request to obtain statistical, technical and other information on Canadian production and marketing problems; fourth, to undertake studies concerning small businesses, particularly for the guidance of government in the development of new policies in this field and
822	HOUSE OF
Low Interest Loans to Small Business for background material for dealing more effectively with the problems of small businesses. Finally, in the course of its work, the section was intended to consult and cooperate with educational institutions, representative business organizations and other private organizations.
These two measures come to mind and there are others which have contributed to creating a better atmosphere for small businesses in Canada. In fact there was such a considerable success in this program that many business people commenced to improve their facilities, to put on extensions to present buildings and to borrow from lending institutions for this purpose. This process created a demand for credit which, along with the other features, used up a great deal of the available credit and sent up the interest rate. I know that other arguments will be advanced from one place and another as to what caused the interest rate to go up. I am not an economist but I do know that when business is good, people are encouraged to expand, to grow, to go into an additional line, to buy larger stocks, and to improve their stores and shops in such a way that they want to borrow money. In borrowing they use up, to a large extent, the available credit facilities and they have done so.
I want to speak for a minute or two about the businesses which did not benefit from this general upsurge and we must admit that there were some, because all businesses did not improve and have not improved. I think they fall into three classes. The first class is those who were already in debt and who found it difficult to get out of debt, even with an improved atmosphere in the business world. Second, there were those who did not improve their position because of the nature of their business. Third, there were those to whom normal credit facilities are denied. I think these are the people to whom this resolution ought to apply. These three classes of people have not benefited by the general improvement in the business situation in Canada. There may be those among the small businessmen who could not "make it go" in any case and those are the difficult type that must be dealt with in considering any general small business loans. In every instance it is a case of applying the rules for each application; but I think we must consider class by class the person to whom a small business loan would apply.
By way of example, I should like to mention the case of a group of persons in whom I have had a continuing interest and on whose behalf I have spoken a good many times in this house. I think their situation


points up a class of people who do not fall into the group who have benefited under the improved business situation. I refer to the operators of tourist establishments. To apply the rules that I have already mentioned:	Is there an urgent situation in
relation to these people? Owing to lack of funds, many tourist operators are not making in their facilities the improvements that are absolutely necessary if they are to keep up with the standard of building and improvement which is being carried on in competing nations. I think particularly of the nation to the south of us. There are great improvements in facilities at border points. We run into situations wherein people heading out for Canada often do not arrive here.
Tourism is the third largest producer of foreign currency in Canada. Notwithstanding the fact that we had in this country in 1958 a direct revenue of at least $394 million from people travelling in Canada from beyond our borders, we had a substantial travel deficit. This is increasing. I might say in passing, Mr. Speaker, that we are hopeful that 1959 will have seen an improvement in the situation. Figures compiled for the first nine months of 1959 indicate that there was an increase of 10 per cent in tourist revenues in this country. I think a great deal of it was brought about by the royal visit because a good many people came to this country who normally would not have done so. I think right here in Ottawa one of the most significant things was the changing of the guard which took place on the lawn of parliament hill last summer and which I understand is to be enlarged and extended. A great many of the people who are visiting the country are greatly attracted to a display of colour such as that which is put on each day during the summer months. In 1958, however, the travel deficit increased by $31 million to a deficit with all countries of $193 million.
In fairness, however, I think we must remember that a travel deficit is created in one main way, namely that more people from Canada are travelling abroad and spending money there, than are coming to Canada. While at first glance this situation seems to be "a bad thing," the fact is that it indicates a prosperity in Canada which encourages and permits Canadians to travel abroad more extensively than ever before. The figures which are included in the travel deficit also include purchases which Canadians have made while abroad, and that factor makes quite a difference in the picture. However, I believe we are not securing a fair share of the world-wide increase in travel and that our facilities have much to do with the situation.

The second test that I have set out is whether it is in the national interest that the tremendous revenue of foreign dollars that we take in from this particular trade should be maintained to its fullest extent in our general world trade picture. I truly believe that it is a matter of urgent national interest.
There has been some talk of putting our house in order for the centennial celebration in 1967. I can think of nothing more urgent when we invite people to come to our country to help us celebrate our hundredth year of existence as a country than to have in this country facilities of which we shall be proud and which we can without any hesitation ask our visitors to accept.
The next question is whether it is justified, to keep government out of private business. Applying this test to the tourist trade as well, I find that some governments in other countries directly enter into the tourist business in order to sustain and to encourage it, and in order to provide facilities which are apparently beyond the reach of their own citizens and those people who care to invest in that country. This intervention is most undesirable in our country. The alternative is to aid and support private interests who are willing to take the risk and are anxious to do so and put in the hard work that is necessary. However, even here in Canada we find that governments-federal, provincial and even municipal-are entering into this field. I think that is not a desirable thing. I think the alternative is to support private interests rather than to have government enter into the field directly.
We know it exists, particularly in the case of provinces where camping grounds are provided on a grand scale. I will admit that camping grounds are a good thing for attracting visitors to this country. Some of our tourist operators perhaps feel they are being undercut. But most of them feel that as long as they bring people to this country, people who cannot afford to stay at a luxury hotel but who can come and bring their small families and camp in one of these camping grounds, then when they come back in a few years when they are established in their business and the children are a little older they will stay at tourist hotels, motels and other accommodations.
The temptation of the provincial governments is to expand beyond just providing camping facilities and go into the restaurant business and the outfitting business with regard to these camps. It is quite a temptation, and in one or two cases the province has come into it and-

speechtext:
Are they doing that in eastern Ontario?

speechtext:
I hope not. There are two cases in Ontario though where the provincial government has built accommodation for restaurants, and they have resisted the temptation to the extent that they have left the operation of these places to private interests. But it is one of those things where as long as the private interests are not providing accommodation, the government feels that they must.
The same thing applies to our national parks. I must admit that so far I have heard no direct criticism, and being a member of the mines, forests and waters committee, I may say that we did make a very close check of the national parks. We found that in several instances there had been, at times in the past, a temptation to provide these facilities which to some extent was resisted. I think it must be resisted as far as possible, because it takes away the possibility of private persons setting up these places. It is very difficult for a person with a small business, with limited capital and no ability to get any, to go into competition with any government, provincial or federal.
The final test that I would apply is the question of the ability of lending institutions to provide normal lending facilities. The reason that the tourist operator has been unable to secure loans from normal institutions is that the business is considered risky by most financial institutions. It is risky because of a short season. It is risky because of the danger of bad weather, a change in operation or poor operation. As a general rule, banks and lending institutions place tourist operations at the bottom of their list. There are so many people who are looking for loans in various fields that unless you come high on the list your chances are never very good.
Just by way of comparison, the tourist business provides to this country almost as much foreign currency as the sale of wheat. It comes after the sale of wheat and is just as important. Yet, quite properly, we spend much of our time in this house attempting to keep our wheat production and income in balance and to keep agriculture generally on an even keel. I often wonder why parliament does give the majority of its attention to one type of business and practically ignores another which is in difficulties and which is getting no assistance. I had thought at different times that perhaps the people who were interested in tourist businesses did not yell loud enough in the house. I have been trying to do so, but I have to admit, Mr. Speaker, that it is quite a job to keep up with such hon. members as the hon. members for Acadia (Mr. Horner), for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg), and for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden), and about forty others in this

I do think, however, that we must give consideration to the provision of loans for small businesses which do not come within the classes I have mentioned, and to that extent I do support the resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to express the support of this party for the principle, the purpose and the spirit of this resolution. From previous debates in this house I am sure a good many hon. members will realize that the C.C.F. has always been particularly concerned with the problems of small business, whether that business be operating in industry or in retailing or in services.
We recognize that small business is a thread in the social fabric that must be kept strong if we are going to retain a democratic form of society. It is for that reason that the C.C.F. over a number of years has, within the caucus itself and within other groups in our movement across Canada, conducted study groups and discussed the problems of small businesses, whether they were in industry or in retailing or in services, with various other groups in one place in Canada and another.

Since the last interesting debate on this question, which I think was early in July of last year, I have had an opportunity, like the rest of the hon. members here, to return to my constituency and meet a good number of business people. I have had the opportunity to meet groups in Nelson, Trail, Ross-land, and other smaller communities in my district. I believe in getting in touch with the people in the various groups in the community and finding out what their particular problems are. I found in almost every case when I had discussions with them that the particular problem at the present time with regard to small business in Canada is its inability to get a suitable type of long term, low interest credit.
I have had some very interesting illustrations brought to my attention. For instance, I met a young man in the contracting business who had returned from overseas after the second world war, had worked for the construction industry and, finally as the result of his ability and initiative, had gathered together a little capital and formed a company which was particularly concerned with contracting for the application of asphalt on the highways which are being built in British Columbia at the present time. Incidentally, these highways are mesmerising some people as to the delinquencies of the social credit government of British Columbia. However, this young man went into business and was getting along very well in a small way, becoming quite well known, fulfilling small contracts and doing an excellent job comparable to those done by the large construction firms usually imported from the United States to do this work. Suddenly he was faced with this difficult credit situation. Another contract came to him, good as gold, one might say. He had the experience, he had the equipment and he had the contract. He went to the bank to borrow, having in the bank at the same time $10,000 worth of this government's bonds, and the bank manager said to him: I am very sorry, but in the circumstances the maximum I can let you have is $500, and you can sell your bonds.

In order to indicate the interest of the royal commission on price spreads in this question I wish to quote briefly from the report, because these gentlemen made a very lengthy study of this problem. I wish to quote from page 59, volume 1 of the report directly beneath the heading "The Problem of the Small Business Firm":
We have pointed out that we have been unable to discover evidence to support the view that the increase in the size of the large firms in the food industries, which has accompanied the general expansion of the market, has resulted in reduced costs and a tendency to reduce prices to consumers.
This is regardless of the fact that a good many people are of the opinion that these large monolithic food distributing mammoths and monopolies are doing a favour to the people of this country. The report goes on to say:
We are disposed to explain this partly in terms of the tendency for large firms to compete in offering services rather than reduction in prices. We find no substantial basis to suppose that if

I think that is a very significant paragraph. And now, if I may, I will read one other paragraph which appears at the conclusion of this particular phase of the report.
At the same time we are concerned about the narrowing opportunities which exist in our economy for individual initiative outside the framework of the large corporations.
So are the members of this group concerned about the narrowing opportunities available. Then the report goes on to say:
The emphasis we have intended in our report is on the widest possible distribution of the gains from efficiency and it is not our wish to suggest procedures which would place on consumers the burden of maintaining high cost firms. Nevertheless, we feel that in order to provide a greater measure of equality of opportunity for the small and efficient firm-
I may point out that there are two things which members of this group do not support: one is laziness, and the other is inefficiency. Let no one think we do. The report goes on:
-in order to provide a greater measure of equality of opportunity for the small and efficient firm, and for the enterprising new firm, greater solicitude should be shown for the small organization and for businesses struggling to become established. In the concluding section of our recommendations we refer to deficiencies in the statistics on small firms, and we recommend that more complete information on the operations of small enterprises should be obtained and made available. This is the first and necessary step in devising action appropriate to the needs of the small business.
It is very strange, but I think it was the session before last when one of the members of this group, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), speaking on this question suggested the very same thing. He put forward the very same proposal, and here we have a royal commission coming to the same conclusion after an extensive investigation; the same conclusion as was reached by this little, valiant band a year previously.
Now I want to say a word on the second volume of this report. These royal commissions are an advantage, because if we read their reports we find they offer evidence and reach conclusions which provide us with guidance as to the course of action we should pursue. I think that guidance is strongly given in support of the resolution which has been moved by the hon. member the name of whose constituency I cannot pronounce, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter).
