I quoted these extracts from volumes I and
II	of the report of the royal commission on price spreads of food products because in the first place I think they indicate clearly the important function that the small businessman-and here particularly we are dealing with retailers-plays in our economy, the service they render, and it also indicates the validity of the argument of those who make representations and proposals for the government to take some action along the lines suggested in this resolution.
I always believe it is wise to keep the house up to date on the thinking of hon. members of this party in this corner of the chamber in order that our position will be understood. I want to place on the record the C.C.F. policy with respect to small business as it was placed on the record by the hon. member for Vancouver East on July 1, 1958, as reported at page 1812 of Hansard:
1.	Broaden the class of loans under the industrial development bank to include a broad coverage of non-industrial enterprises such as the service industries, distributive trades, etc.
[Mr. Herridge .1
2.	Increase the capitalization of the industrial development bank to accommodate increased lending, investing and guaranteeing of loans.
3.	Amend the Bank Act to allow chartered banks to lend money or make advances to qualifying small business upon the security, mortgage or hypothecation of real or immovable property. May I say that this would be in addition to the special exceptions which have already been made in this respect under the National Housing Act, 1954, and the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
4.	Guarantee term loans by chartered banks to small business against losses up to 10 per cent of the total amount of such loans made by any bank. May I add there that the figure of 10 per cent was chosen by our group because the same percentage is operative under similar guarantees, for example, with respect to farm improvement loans.
5.	Enable chartered banks to sell mortgages securing such term loans to the industrial development bank in the same way in which the banks are enabled to sell housing mortgages to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Furthermore, ensure that banks can receive advances from the Bank of Canada using such mortgages as eligible security in the same way in which they can receive advances from the Bank of Canada using housing mortgages as security.
I briefly put those five points on the record so hon. members would know our policy with respect to small business. Once again I urge the government to take some action.
Last year toward the conclusion of the debate on this question the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) spoke and if I remember correctly he suggested that government policy in establishing the small business section of the Department of Trade and Commerce would be to provide a clearing house of ideas and also to provide reports and bulletins for small business in Canada, to make available the necessary statistics, a course of action we advocated two years previously and which the royal commission also spoke of as being necessary. He went on to say it would also have the purpose of undertaking studies and consulting with various educational institutions and other groups with a view to assisting the welfare and interests of the small business people in this country.
I think the mover of the resolution would agree that we hope to hear from the minister before the debate concludes this evening as to how far the government has gone with respect to the implementation of the purposes of the small business section of the minister's department. It is obvious that there has not been any effective action taken to date or otherwise we would not travel around the country and hear a considerable percentage of the small businessmen complaining of their difficulties as a result of-I do not like the term "tight money"; I dislike the word "tight" and I think the description is incorrect-a shortage of cash and credit. They would not be complaining about the situation if the small business section and its activities had done

something to promote their interest since the minister spoke last year. In conclusion I want once again to emphasize our concern with this important group in our society and their welfare, and say that we anticipate an excellent speech from the Minister of Trade and Commerce before the debate on this resolution concludes this evening, and to hear the results of the high hopes he raised in the house for this session when he made his speech last July.

maintopic: PROVISION OF LOW INTEREST LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise in this debate to speak on this resolution because this is a matter which I have always considered of paramount importance and one which I think should have the fullest support of this house and the government. I also find that I am in agreement with the principle of the resolution and with almost all that has been said thus far in the debate as I am sure most hon. members are.
Certainly, as far as the question of whether or not the government of Canada is encroaching upon any private domain by entering into the field of special credit assistance to small business is concerned, I believe everyone will agree it is a time-honoured principle that the first and primary duty of government in credit assistance is to help out in the situation where the ordinary doors of capital are not open to a borrower.
Where there are sectors in the economy which do not have access to bank loans, mortgage company loans and other credit sources, I think it is the place of any government to step in to fill that credit gap. That has been the principle behind legislation extending credit to farmers, fishermen and other sectors of the economy. Prior to the development of farmer's and fishermen's credit facilities it was difficult for those groups to obtain loans.
Private capital seeks out the borrower who seems to represent the best risk, who can put up security which is most easily liquefied in case of default of the loan and, above all, seeks a loan which requires the least supervision and administration. For this obvious reason a businessman or salaried person in an urban centre who enjoys a relatively more stable income and who resides close to the lender's vaults finds it much easier to borrow than the rural dweller. A mortgage company or bank which can lend in the city looks askance at the farmer or fisherman whose security for a loan is not so easily liquefied in case of default and whose income is subject to the whims and perils of the weather, the market, or the other thorns of fate that beset the rural dweller.
Low Interest Loans to Small Business
This credit gap was partially closed by the legislation which provided bank guarantees for farmers and fishermen and by similar legislation. We have this type of help from both federal and provincial governments. Under the same principle we have government intervention to meet a gap in the credit facilities offered by private capital for house building. The National Housing Act was passed to provide funds for good housing in every part of Canada. Before the institution of this form of credit the home owner himself had to have at least 40 per cent of the cash requirement to build a house. Private mortgage fund sources were limited either by law or by practice to 60 per cent of the value of the property which would act as security for the loan. This type of lending could never have provided the houses needed to house the great increase in our population since the war.
One of the most important provisions of the National Housing Act was that, in addition to providing a guaranteed type of loan through an approved lender, it also provided that in areas where private capital was not too willing to act, a borrower could make a direct application to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I know personally a great number of home owners from rural areas and small towns who were declined funds by approved lenders, who could then turn to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and obtain the funds which they needed to build houses. Surely, in a situation such as that it is the duty of government to provide funds where otherwise they would not be available.
When legislation is introduced to assist small business the priority on available funds should be given to the small businessman who is having the most difficulty in obtaining funds from the regular channels. One of the best illustrations of the limitation of available capital to some small businesses is that given by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) in his suggestion that the tourist industry could benefit largely from legislation of this kind. The tourist motel or hotel proprietor, at least in my province, cannot build under bank financing. What he needs is long term mortgage financing, which is not available from the banks. On the other hand, if he applies to the conventional mortgage companies he might be able to borrow 60 per cent of what he needs, which is a relatively small fraction of the big expenditure required. Hostelry is not a very high income-producing investment in many areas particularly for the small motel, and the conventional mortgage assistance that is available is not satisfactory to do the job of

Low Interest Loans to Small Business financing tourist accommodation. The repayment risk is often higher on a motel or hotel than on an ordinary dwelling loan.
A commercial building mortgage is usually considered to be a little more risky than a loan on a dwelling. The loan requires more supervision; it costs more to administrate in many instances than a dwelling loan. The practical result is that if mortgage funds are available at all for tourist accommodation, they represent too small a portion of the capital required. There is little encouragement in our present capital lending system, as regards hotels and motels for the tourist business.
In some instances some provinces have stepped in to help, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. In Nova Scotia loans are available through the department of industry for the building of hotel accommodation, and tourist accommodation in general, but the capital the province has to offer for this is, perforce, very thinly spread and, as in the case of the conventional mortgages, the motel owner in Nova Scotia must have a very substantial amount of cash on hand before he can consider building. He must have 40 per cent or over in some cases, or he must be able to find a private mortgage, usually a short term one, to finance his building. It is not, to my mind, the type of encouragement that this very important industry should have. I am sure the department of trade and industry in my province would very warmly welcome long term capital to assist in the building of tourist accommodation.
The reluctance of private capital to finance tourist building is bridling a national industry of first importance and limitless potential. I believe one of the first priorities for money made available for small business should go to the motel owner or innkeeper. Surely, there are very few spheres of business activity which so affect everyone in the community as the tourist business. The tourist dollar makes a wide circle once it starts to travel, and the man who makes it possible for us to earn that tourist dollar in many instances is the motel or hotel operator. I believe it is in everybody's interest to encourage him not only in financing but in any other way we can.
The reason raised by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka as to the propriety of government setting up tourist accommodation in some of our national parks interests me. In fact, the situation is that in some of our parks, particularly in areas where the season is not too long, it is not economically practical for free enterprise to build tourist accommodation. Cape Breton Highlands national park, a large part of which is in my riding,

was visited by 189,000 people this year. It boosted the tourist industry in Cape Breton island by 39 per cent last year and by 17 per cent this year. It is a very important business in Nova Scotia. The hotel accommodation in the Cape Breton Highlands national park in the first instance was built by the government of Canada and leased to the province of Nova Scotia. It would be pleasant if we could say that if this had not been done private enterprise would have come in and built the accommodation and provided the first lure, if you like, for tourists to the province; but that probably would not have been so. Now that so many guests have started to come in as a result of this government investment, then private enterprise, hotel and motel operators, were able to build accommodation to provide for the new people who were coming in. But the first investment had to be made by the government. I believe it was a wise investment; it certainly has proved so in dollars and cents in my riding.
I have spoken of the tourist industry. But the best illustration of the general need for small business credits is to be found in the rural areas throughout Canada. The primary producer on the farm, or engaged in lumbering or fishing, whatever he is doing, suffers many handicaps. He has to travel for his medical and other professional services. If he does not, then he must pay double the cost to have those services brought to him. His labour and products are generally at the mercy of the shifting values of demand and supply, while his brother in the city is protected by a union or association, or a gentleman's agreement. He braves the sea and the wind, or the flood and the drought, or the heat or the cold.
But all these troubles are as nothing compared with the discrimination he faces when he wants to borrow some money. The mortgage companies are of very little assistance in the rural areas, as I have said. They prefer to lend in the cities. The farmers and fishermen have been greatly assisted by federal and provincial loan legislation; but the lumberman still finds it very difficult to obtain long term money to modernize his plant or to bring in new equipment. The small sawmill operator in many parts of Canada is a very important rural employer. He turns out a necessary product and I am sure, in my riding, if there were more encouragement to the sawmill operator to expand he would develop a very vital local industry. The provisions of the industrial development bank are of very little help to the lumberman, and since he is not manufacturing a finished or semi-finished product he does not come within the aegis of the help provided by the province.

There is another rural businessman who should have priority for loan assistance, namely the small packager or processor of farm and fish products. An important aspect of the Nova Scotia fish industry is salt fish processing. We have growing export markets for good salt fish. Most of this product comes from shore fishermen and is handled by small buyers who operate small plants in the main fishing areas. Those small buyers provide the chief market for the shore fishermen. They supply salted fish at a competitive price for the export trade, chiefly with the West Indies. Their capital requirements are not large, but it is almost impossible for them to borrow long term capital.
Every small businessman will welcome legislation that will help him to secure long term capital, but in particular such help is needed in the rural areas. The rural businessman is the real Cinderella of the credit world. He is the last to obtain money when there is lots of it and he is the first to feel the squeeze when money is tight. I think we will all agree that the first credit help to small business should go to the businessman for whom ordinary capital doors are hardest to open. And first in this category are the merchants, the co-operatives, the small rural processors and packagers, the lumbermen, and the contracting tradesmen who service our rural areas.
There has been some discussion in the debate so far, some suggestions put forward, as to the way in which money could be made available to the small businessman, and the ways that would help him best. I understand that, some years ago it was suggested by the retail merchants association that a good way to assist retailers would be along the lines of the loans now extended to farmers and fishermen. They asked that the government should guarantee 10 per cent of a bank loan up to $25,000. The government puts up no money, but guarantees a bank loan to the extent of 10 per cent over a period of five or six years. A plan of this nature would be very helpful and could be accomplished without a complex administration because the work would be done, as it is now for the farmers and fishermen, by the bankers.
However, even more useful to the small businessman would be a form of guaranteed mortgage loans. Under present laws, building mortgage funds are not available through the banks. I think, myself, that the chief financial problem that faces the small businessman stems from the fact that he must have so much of his capital tied up in fixtures, plant, buildings and so on and that he is short of capital for inventory and other current purposes. If mortgage lenders were
Low Interest Loans to Small Business encouraged to look more kindly on commercial building loans amortized over 10 or 15 year periods, a large part of the financial problems of many of our small businessmen would be removed or greatly ameliorated. This also raises a general question as to whether there is any longer a need to prohibit banks from lending on the security of real property. I believe the time has come when we should re-examine that rule in the light of modern business conditions, particularly from the point of view of small business loans.
We have made an exception already in the case of the National Housing Act loans. Where a certain percentage of the loan is guaranteed by the government, the banks are permitted to lend money on the security of real property. It is very common in the United States for banks to accept security of all types for loans, including buildings, cars, furniture or any other security that is offered.
There is another agency whose scope could be widened very easily to provide more credit service and that is the industrial development bank. The industrial development bank was incorporated by act of parliament in 1944 and commenced operations on November 1 of that year. Its functions are described in the preamble of the act which set up the bank, and I quote:
Whereas it is desirable to establish an industrial development bank to promote the economic welfare of Canada by increasing the effectiveness of monetary action through ensuring the availability of credit to industrial enterprises which may reasonably be expected to prove successful if a high level of national income and employment is maintained, by supplementing the activities of other lenders and by providing capital assistance to industry with particular consideration to the financing problems of small enterprises-
The chief purpose of this act was to make money available to those to whom it would not otherwise be available, particularly small businesses. The president of the industrial development bank is the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. J. E. Coyne, and the directors of the bank are the same as those of the Bank of Canada. The bank was set up with a $25 million capitalization, which was provided by the Bank of Canada.
I have always felt, like the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter), that the industrial development bank left a lot to be desired, particularly with regard to its functions in the field of small business. It is true that over the last three years the services of the industrial development bank have greatly improved.
I notice from the bank's annual report that in 1955 a total of 221 loans were granted by the bank. This had grown, by 1959, a few years later, to 599 loans. For example, in
830	HOUSE OF
Low Interest Loans to Small Business my own province, in 1955, there were only 4 loans granted by the industrial development bank and in 1956 there were a mere 7. In 1959 the number had reached 33. In terms of the money involved there was $252,000 lent by the bank in 1955, that is in Nova Scotia, and in 1959 the total had reached $1,369,000. I noticed when the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo was speaking that he mentioned that in all the years the bank has been in operation, I believe some 15 years, there have been only 14 businesses in Newfoundland that were able to take advantage of it. It is interesting to note that of these 14, there were 7 loans granted in 1959 and only 7 in all the previous years of the bank's operation. This shows that the industrial development bank has been trying to make more money available.
However, there is one specific trouble with the industrial development bank and that is that it does not seem to like small loans. If one looks at pages 6 and 7 of the bank report, it will be seen that of the $30.5 million the bank now has loaned, loans of $5,000 or less account for only $105,000; loans between $5,000 and $25,000 amount to only $3.9 million. If you total these two figures and consider loans of $25,000 or under, they account for $4 million and there is $26.5 million tied up in larger loans. This is the problem the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo has found, as I have found in so far as the industrial development bank is concerned. People in my riding, who live in rural areas and small towns have told me they have found the bank rather snooty.
Some of my constituents, for example, have applied to the bank for a loan for use in the forestry industry, which is an important industry in my riding. I notice the bank's report indicates there has been only one forestry loan granted between the years 1955 and 1959. I am told that people from rural areas who seek a loan of this nature meet a rather cool reception at the bank. It seems also that the bank gives the cold shoulder to the man who wants to borrow money to build or modernize a small food-processing plant, such as in the salt fish industry. I think the bank could greatly extend its service by looking again at its small loan policy. Perhaps the bank should consider setting up a special department to handle loans under $25,000. At the moment, there seems to be as much red tape involved in a simple mortgage loan of $10,000 as there would be for a loan of $200,000.
I have been following the progress of a constituent of mine who has applied for a small loan to assist in constructing a salt fish processing plant. The bank required that an
[Mr. MacLellan.l

appraiser drive some 90 miles from Sydney to appraise the building and fixtures. They required a special audit. They required long range forecasts of prices and markets and practically wanted a guarantee of the price of fish five years from now. They wanted an architect's drawing of a $7,000 or $8,000 one storey building, and so on. If and when my constituent does obtain his small loan from the industrial development bank he will have paid heavily for all of this appraising and information and I doubt whether the loan is worth the trouble. I wonder whether the industrial development bank would find it feasible to have small loans of this type processed by the local banks, particularly where the borrowers are from small towns or rural areas.

1 know, but I believe it would be a breach of confidence if I gave that information. It is quite a small loan. In the case to which I have just referred, I am sure the local bank manager would have processed that loan in one quarter of the time that was required by the office of the industrial development bank, some 250 miles away in Halifax. The banker would know at a glance whether the proposition was sound and feasible. He knows the man's history and character. He would know whether or not he is a good credit risk. Certainly long before this the man of whom I speak could have had a decision upon whether or not the loan application would be accepted by the bank.
There is another consideration also. The bank manager is able to advise and counsel the applicant. I should like to see some consideration given to having local bank managers in rural areas act as agents of the industrial development bank for small loans.
The industrial development bank, like every other bank, wants to show a little profit and above all it wants to preserve its assets. But it differs from other banks in that it is set up with public funds to serve a special purpose. One of those purposes is to provide credit to the small businessman who is operating an industrial enterprise and who cannot get funds elsewhere. Most small businessmen seem to think there could be a great improvement in the exercise of this responsibility.

In conclusion, may I say that I agree with this resolution and support it. I think that small business could be helped greatly by setting up a new agency which would make loans available either by bank guarantees or, as in the case of the National Housing Act, by long term mortgage loans. Improvement could also be effected by making existing agencies more flexible and more attuned to the problems of small industry in the nation.

maintopic: PROVISION OF LOW INTEREST LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
At the
outset, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) for introducing this resolution urging the government to give consideration to legislation designed to help small business in which I would also include the tourist operators. Those who belong in this classification are severely handicapped because of the seasonal character of their business and yet they are responsible for much of the wealth brought in by tourists and which has not cost the public treasury any money.
Last year the Canadian tourist association presented to the government a brief asking for legislation designed to relieve Canada's tourist industry of the serious disability caused by lack of financial credit and to get the government to provide funds for much needed loans for expansion and modernization of facilities and buildings to enable them to compete effectively in this particular business from which, directly or indirectly, everyone benefits.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) asked the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) just a few moments ago whether he knew of any instances in which tourist operators had actually been handicapped by want of capital, and the hon. member replied that he did not have figures. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I know of instances of tourist operators in Fort William being forced to get out of the business because they were unable to borrow money for the purpose of modernizing their facilities.
The government's attitude toward the suggestion of loans was that it considers technical assistance but no money. This technical help may be of some value but, without money, all the advice in the world in the majority of instances would mean practically nothing. I think that the government could assist small businesses by guaranteeing loans to the bank in a way similar to that in which it is now providing funds for the con-structon of homes through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
When a similar resolution was introduced in July, 1955 by the hon. member for Parry
Low Interest Loans to Small Business Sound-Muskoka who spoke this afternoon- and very well indeed, I may say-it was well received by all parties, but it met the same fate as many other well-meaning proposals. It was talked out because this government did not want it to come to a vote for fear perhaps that it would unmask some hypocritical double-talkers. Where the life of the government is not at stake I think it should perhaps be possible for resolutions or bills before the house to be the subject of a free vote. I do not pretend to be an authority on parliamentary procedure, but it seems to me that the system of allowing private members to speak out and vote according to their thinking would be a decided improvement over our present custom of voting as we are told.
It should be remembered that the small businesses of the country-in which I include all classes of merchants, garages, filling stations, grocery and fruit stores, drug stores et cetera-probably account for 60 per cent of internal trade in Canada, upon which the well-being of the people and the prosperity of the country depend to a great extent. It is therefore not inconsistent to ask the government for consideration of certain financial problems which have to do with expansion of facilities of small business to enable them to compete with huge chain stores which are now in the process of driving the small businessman out of business.
When speaking on the subject of small business during the debate on the supply estimates of his department during the 1958 session the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) made the following statement and I quote from Hansard, page 4536:

The hon. member for Vancouver East has just voiced his usual interjection and added his usual intelligence to this debate. In answer to him I will say I am 100 per cent in favour of this resolution, as is this present government from any indication which they have given to the people of this country. But in looking at this resolution I think we have first of all to answer the question: is there a need for government lending to small business? In order to answer that question I feel we have to look at the business world in general.

Low Interest Loans to Small Business
May I say that I am one of those who do not believe in government interference in the business world unless it is absolutely necessary because I feel that in a democratic system the individuals and those other components comprising the state owe a duty to our system in the same way as does the government. There are institutions in our system which lend money and which perform other functions of a financial nature for other aspects and segments of our system. First of all, we should examine those aspects and determine whether or not these institutions are fulfilling their duty toward our democratic system. In that regard we must look not only at big business but at moneylenders and our banking practices.
In the field of big business, because of the large capital and other resources available, demands can be made which not only must be but invariably are met by the people with whom such undertakings deal. This is done without regard to other aspects of our economy. We could look, for instance, at the large chain store which is capable of offering a certain quantity of goods for a certain price and which, in turn, could return a handsome profit to its shareholders but which in spite of all this does a certain amount of harm to other people and other businesses engaged in the same method of operation. We can look at the banks and ask ourselves: are they fulfilling the functions that they were designed to fulfil in our democratic and free enterprise system or have they become more concerned with making money for their shareholders, forgetting the services which they are morally obligated to provide under our system? That is the general picture of the argument that may be put forward in support of this resolution as far as the country as a whole is concerned.
Now I should like for a few minutes to become somewhat more parochial and concern myself with my own constituency of Winnipeg North. Those who live in Winnipeg North are primarily wage earners and small shop keepers. There is no main business and no main manufacturing industry in my constituency and, therefore, the problems of the small businessman have been brought to my attention as no other problems have been. Since my election I have contacted all the druggists in my constituency, nearly 80 per cent of the operators of corner grocery stores, hardware stores, small chain stores, dry goods stores and so on. I have discussed their problems with them. They pointed out to me over and over again that the main problem confronting them as far as getting ahead in the financial world was concerned was the problem of capital.

I queried many of these businessmen in my constituency some five years ago, in 1955, and I found it interesting to make a comparison between conditions obtaining then and their present day situation. I found in my own constituency, and I am sure this applies in other ridings, that those small businesses- and here I use the word "small" as meaning small, the corner grocery stores, drug stores and so on-in 1955 employed on the average three people in addition to the proprietor. In 1960 on the average they employ only the proprietor and, in some cases, a part-time delivery boy. I also learned that their turnover and gross sales increased in 1960 over 1955 but their net return and their incomes have been lower. All this has been brought about by competition with large stores that are in the advantageous position of being able to buy in quantity thereby achieving reductions and discounts that the small businessman cannot obtain.
At this point I should like to cite an example. One corner grocer told me that his jobber could sell him a certain brand of soap at 71 cents a package. The mark-up figure on a percentage basis would bring his selling price to 79 cents. However, the grocer was able to go to one of the large general stores in his locality and buy a case of this brand of soap at 60 cents a package and sell it for 69 cents, 2 cents under the price at which his jobber was able to sell it to him.
I do not say we should have government legislation to interfere with this because that is part of our free enterprise system. I do say, however, that those who offer large discounts owe a duty to our democratic system just as the government owes a duty to them. I say they are not fulfilling that duty when they are making things so tough on the smaller businessman that he is no longer in a position to compete.
Those who advocate the practice of free enterprise to the ultimate limit might say this is a good thing but I say it is not, because in this nation we have far more people employed by and dependent upon smaller businesses than we have in relation to larger businesses.
One could lead the discussion into other fields. We do not have to stay with the grocery trade, the garages, small manufacturers, fishermen, lumbermen, and so on. I am very glad that this resolution is worded in the broadest possible terms but I suggest that if private enterprise and our financial institutions are not doing the job they ought to do and which they are morally obliged to do under our system, then the government must step in and provide loans to those who otherwise would not obtain them.

The hon. member for Fort William rather chastised the government for doing nothing since its election to office. I would remind the hon. member that this government assumed office on June 21, 1957, and in the time previous to that we had 22 years of Liberal rule during which the Liberals, as far as I am aware, did nothing for small business. Indeed, it might be said that they did more for big business in the United States than they did for any business in Canada.
I was impressed by the remarks made today by the hon. members for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Aiken) and Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan). They dwelt at length upon the requirements of the Bank Act and amendments that may have to be made to that statute in order to allow small businessmen to borrow money from the bank. Their arguments, I feel, have covered that ground far more adequately than could any of mine.
I feel there is a great deal of merit to this resolution. It is something which if brought into effect would certainly assist those in my constituency who today find themselves in a position where they could become bigger businessmen except for the fact that they cannot find the capital which will meet their needs.
As I pointed out earlier, I feel that if those institutions in our economy that should provide this service are not providing it the government of this country should step in and make that assistance available. In answer to those hon. members who questioned me earlier I would say that I am in wholehearted support of this resolution and my only regret is that it was not brought in by the hon. member who sponsored it when his party was in a position to do more about it than it is today.

When we examine the question in that light we begin to grasp the immensity of the problem. This is not a matter like those dealt with on earlier occasions when the government has provided credit for one purpose or another. This is something that will tax the entire resources of the country.
There has been an admitted storage of capital in Canada. Everybody recognizes that fact. We have heard it over and over again. Indeed, one of the criticisms of the opposition has been that the government, by interfering in things, is using up too much of the credit in one way or another. The resolution goes on to say that:
The government should give urgent consideration to the provision of some means whereby low interest loans may be made available to small business.
There is only one interpretation of that resolution that one can come to. It would amount to setting up some government institution to provide loans to small business and at low rates of interest which, I presume, would mean lower than the average rate of interest in the country at the present time. At least, that is the assumption one would come to when the hon. member specifically mentions low interest rates. This again means that some sort of subsidy would have to be

paid in order for the government to borrow the money. It will have to go out into the money markets and borrow the money and set up such an agency, as I have already pointed out.
When one considers that what they are going to provide credit for constitutes some 80 per cent or 90 per cent of the business in Canada, he can begin to see something of the amount of money they would have to raise in order to do that particular thing. One thing is perfectly obvious to me. When the house rose at six o'clock, I had been stating that I did not believe the immensity of the proposition contained in this resolution had been recognized. It is true, and is a fact, that small business as referred to in this resolution would certainly constitute some 80 per cent or 90 per cent of the total business in Canada. The proposition set forth here is that the government should establish some sort of institution which would lend out money to small business at low rates of interest. I was further saying that this, of course, went far beyond what it appeared to do at first glance because it meant going into the whole question of the allocation of the existing credit we have.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house some of the remarks of Mr. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada, contained in the annual report of that institution for the year 1958. These remarks deal, to a large extent, with this situation. This whole question, then, goes back to what has been commonly referred to as tight money or a shortage of capital in the country, and here is what Mr. Coyne had to say about it:
The experience of 1955-1957 is, I hope, fresh in our minds. In the conditions which were then experienced, and which may recur, many people feel that they do not have a fair opportunity to obtain access to capital and credit for what they regard as necessary and proper purposes. The impression arises that some borrowers, particularly in the larger category, are able to do better than others and that there is undesirable discrimination and misdirection in the allocation of resources or in the ability to command resources. As I have emphasized many times in the past, monetary policy does not create these problems and can do little itself to alleviate them.
I think that brings to the attention of the house something of the immensity of the problem. I pointed out earlier in my remarks that the government certainly has given great consideration to this matter. I was rather surprised, as I said, at the bland acceptance by
Low Interest Loans to Small Business the house of this proposition as something new, something that had not been considered, and that should still be considered in such general terms. I feel it is rather useless to go on urging the government to do one thing or another unless there is some specific course to be followed. I do not believe any case at all has been made out for the propositions that have been advanced, of which there have been only two so far as I am aware, one of which has been that we should expand the industrial development bank to meet this need and the other suggestion, which seems to be implicit in the resolution, that it would be necessary to set up some new sort of institution for the government to carry on this allocation of credit.
I have not heard anybody hazard any sort of guess as to what this institution might have to be capitalized at or from what source the money would come. It seems quite clear to me, as I said before, that there is a shortage of capital in the country. We cannot, under any circumstances at the present time, meet all the needs of all the businesses in Canada. If we were going to set up some sort of institution of this nature, it is quite clear that one small businessman would be able to get a loan from it and another would not. In other words, one man in one block would be subsidizing his competitor down the street, thus helping to put himself out of business. I do not think any such scheme as that is going to work at all or be of any value to the country.
The Prime Minister, in his remarks made it quite clear that he felt very much the same about the situation. Here is what he said when speaking to the nation on the program "The Nation's Business", over the C.B.C. on October 1, 1959:
It is obvious that if we make more credit available to small borrowers, it can be done in one of two ways; either a greater money supply must be created, or what is available must be more equitably apportioned.
He went on in that same vein in those remarks to the nation. Later on in his speech, he said:
Accordingly, one place to look for the solution of the present problem of credit is in the allocation of the total supply of credit available. I think, because it is from the chartered banks in the cities, the towns and the villages, that the lifeblood of Canada's economic growth comes, that banks should realize that when they say "no", money becomes a problem and a difficulty.
Then, he went on further to say:
Perhaps one answer is for the banks to reconsider their lending policies and rearrange their outstanding loans to the end that some larger borrowers will be taking less so that smaller borrowers can get more.
I think that sums up very well the crux of the matter. I should like to examine now

The other day the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) accused the Prime Minister of saying that the banks were discriminating against small borrowers. Of course, when asked for the quotation out of the speech from which I have just read, the Leader of the Opposition was not able to give it. However, I believe the Prime Minister did bring validly to the attention of the banks these facts and I believe this statement from him has had some influence on the allocation of credit by the banks. This is one means that the government has of dealing with the banks and dealing with financial policy, that is to state publicly the position of the government and the policy of the government in anticipation that the banks will carry out their wishes and no legislation will be required. The Prime Minister made it quite clear that if legislation was at any time required to protect the interests of the small borrowers he would certainly recommend to the country that it be passed.
There are two or three things in here that I think are of great importance in the allocation of credit. This is >a publication called the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada. It is a quarterly publication and this is the one for October, 1959. It shows, and I quote at random, December 31, 1958. dealing with various lines of credit and showing the amount that the banks have in authorized lines of credit in excess of $100,000, the total amounts authorized under that category were $4,457 million. The interesting thing about this figure is that of that total amount oustanding, the amount that had actually been lent to these people was $1,821 million. In other words, 59 per cent of the money that had been allocated by the banks to large borrowers in excess of $100,000 was actually in the bank and had not been loaned.
I think that is something to which the banks should direct themselves, and I think that was the intent of the Prime Minister when he spoke to the banks and told them they should make a better allocation of the money than that and have more regard for the small borrowers. As I have said before, I have no doubt that the advice he passed along will be studied by the banks. I am sure if one were to have the most up to date records, which are not available yet, he would see there had been a change in this regard.
There is one other thing I should like to look at about which I believe there is room for improvement in connection with the allocation of the money supply we have now. I spoke earlier about the way in which the

National Housing Act had been changed and how the banks had gone into mortgage lending. They have, at the present time, some $900 million-odd tied up in that line of credit, which is long term mortgage credit, and which has taken that money out of the current supply available for business. I feel this has restricted the supply somewhat and so was partly responsible-it certainly must have had some effect upon the situation.
The other thing that was done around the same time was the amendment of the Bank of Canada Act in 1954. At that time all that the banks were required to keep on hand as liquid assets was around 5 per cent of deposits. When the Bank of Canada Act was amended in 1954 that figure was increased to 8 per cent. Power was also given to the Bank of Canada to increase that figure to 12 per cent if they saw fit to do so. The Bank of Canada subsequently increased that figure to 12 per cent and indeed, although they did not have any statutory power to go beyond that figure, by voluntary arrangement with the banks and by using their moral suasion on the banks, they prevailed on the banks to raise the figure to 15 per cent.
I do not know whether that figure could safely be reduced and still afford protection to the depositors of the bank but it seems to me that a further 10 per cent increase in the total of the liquid asset reserves of the banks-in 1954 it was only 5 per cent and at the present time they are keeping on hand 15 per cent-has taken a good deal of the available money supply out of circulation. It seems to me that is something to which we might well direct our attention as a possible solution to the problem of making more credit available.
In addition to these things I have mentioned so far as aiding small business is concerned, may I say that I do not believe that providing direct loans to small business is the only means of aiding them by any stretch of the imagination. Certainly the United States has been mentioned many times in the debate. The experience down there was that advice was every bit as important as a direct loan. In many cases it was lack of knowledge and/or lack of efficiency that was causing the financial difficulties of some small business.
Some of the figures that I have been able to obtain from the small business branch which has been set up under the Department of Trade and Commerce would indicate how that branch and its services have been welcomed by small business generally. Here are a few of the publications they have now made available to small business

in order to assist them in addition to providing various courses of instruction and so on. They are providing pamphlets on management aids for small manufacturers, technical aids for small manufacturers, small marketers' aids, small business management series, starting a management of business series, and a small business bulletin series. Since its inception this publication program has dealt with over 245 different topics and over 6 million of these management publications have been distributed up to the middle of last year.
In addition to its publications program the small business administration has a management development program. Through this program it co-sponsors management educational courses with educational institutions and helps management clinics and seminars. According to the last report of the small business administration 19,000 small businessmen attended 595 courses conducted at 210 educational institutions.
Another part of this over-all educational program of the small business administration is its counselling and conference service offering practical and sound advice on sound management principles. Management conferences are co-sponsored by the small business administration in conjunction with local chambers of commerce, banks, trade associations and civic groups. I could go on but I am sure that branch is making its opinions known to businessmen on their own.
With regard to the other actions that have been taken by the government and that have been of direct benefit to small business, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) brought some of them to the attention of the house this afternoon in a forceful and, in my opinion, accurate way. He mentioned the loans that had been made available for houses which certainly had an effect, not only on small business directly by the products that they were able to supply in the building of houses but of course they also help small business. They put more money into the hands of the Canadian public and therefore gave them greater purchasing power which also had a great effect on the small businessman because it is quite evident that even during the recession we had and have now come through the purchasing power at the retail level kept up very well.
Another factor that led to the keeping up of that purchasing power was the increased unemployment insurance benefits which is another instance where the government policy has had a direct bearing on small business. It also put into effect a winter works program which has helped again in the ways I have
Low Interest Loans to Small Business mentioned before, not only by helping the people who are supplying the goods but by putting more money into the hands of the people who were working on the program and so helping to stimulate small business.
I could go on at great length to mention other measures that the government has taken in that regard but I would conclude by summing up and saying this, as I have said before. I do not believe that the immensity of this problem has been recognized by hon. members generally. I think it is wrong to go on urging the government to do something unless there is a specific and profitable course that can be followed. The Prime Minister has made a statement on this matter. As I have shown, the government has taken action in many respects. No new proposals have been made, surprisingly enough, in this debate this afternoon. I find that there is a complete lack of new proposals.
It becomes perfectly obvious then that we are going to be confronted with this problem of a shortage of capital in Canada for some time to come. There has been a chronic shortage over the years and there certainly is no easy or simple solution to it. While it is always very nice to be able to climb on the bandwagon and to say yes, it would be nice to give loans to small business and certainly nobody could be opposed to the principle of such a scheme, in the absence of any proposition that I can see before the house of a nature that is going to succeed in providing capital on any proper or equitable basis for small business, I feel very strongly that it would be absolutely wrong to start any program that is going to start making loans available to some small businesses and not to others and that may be the only result of the government's interfering at this time and setting up another agency.
We simply cannot make available all the capital that is required. Therefore, in the instances that I have mentioned I believe that we should see what we can do toward making a better allocation of what is available in the banks at the present time. We could see whether possibly the liquid assets ratio of the banks could be lowered. I believe those are two distinct possibilities where we could take some constructive action. But as to setting up a new agency to make loans available to small business, I repeat that it could only have the effect of discriminating against some and I feel it would be wrong for the government to embark on such a policy.

Mr. Speaker, this is the reply of the Minister of Finance to a question dealing directly with one of the planks of the Progressive Conservative platform in 1957 and 1958. We recognize even now how often and how loudly the Prime Minister attacked tight money in 1957 and 1958, and how he talked of high interest rates. Yet today we find the interest rates are even higher than they were then. Tight money is now tighter than it was then. Surely, if the problem existed in 1957 and in 1958, it exists now. Yet we have people saying that the problem is too big to tackle, and that maybe there should be some other way of going about it. It was only last weeek that the Minister of Finance stood in his place in this house and said that the Conservative government has honoured all its promises. As I say, that was only last week. I listened too to the hon. member for In-verness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan). It may be true that the number of loans made by the industrial development bank in the last three years have been greater than in 1956; but I suggest again that this increase in the amount of money loaned is largely due to categories which were added to this act in the year 1956.
I was a little disturbed by the comments made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Smith). Today we are discussing small business, and I believe it is only fair that before continuing such a debate as this we should try to find a definition of small business. I should like to refer to a few of the definitions which have been given in this house. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) speaking in this house has tried to define small business. At page 1818 of Hansard, volume 2, 1958 he is on record as saying:
My interpretation of a small business in need of government interest and concern is a business not necessarily of a certain size or volume with regard to its assets, but a business in which there is some relationship between ownership and management. It may be a business consisting of $5,000 or $10,000 of assets; it may go as high as half a million dollars depending on the type of enterprise.
Then there was the definition given by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) on page 1969 of the same volume:
A large business is able to accumulate capital by the issuance of shares on the market and bonds and debentures, and things of that kind. The type of business that we speak of has no access to that capital in the same way because of its local and personal management and the lack of general knowledge by the public concerning the operation of the business in question.
Then again, there was the definition given by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) as reported on page 1994:
The experience of the small business administration has got down as far as loans of from $6,000 to $10,000 for businesses that have assets of from $25,000 to $50,000. The point that has been raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. MacLean) certainly does require a certain amount of definition.
I believe that a definition of small business can be found in the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) as reported at page 4535 of Hansard of September 3, 1958:
Small business is a large and important segment of the Canadian economy in terms of its contribution to employment and national output and its worth in the life of many communities. More than four fifths of all manufacturing establishments in the country have fewer than 50 employees and account for over one sixth of the total selling value of factory shipments.
The minister then went on to state the objectives of the small business branch in these terms:
1.	To act as a clearing house in referring inquiries of small business to the appropriate departments

of the Canadian government or provincial and municipal governments and to various other organizations and institutions;
2.	to compile and distribute bulletins and reports on topics of general interest to small business including information on government procurement;
3.	to assist small business on request to obtain statistical, technical and other information on management, production and marketing problems;
4.	to undertake studies concerning small business, particularly for guidance of the government in developing new policies in this field and as background material for dealing more effectively with the problems of small business;
5.	in the course of its work, to consult and co-operate with educational institutions, representative business associations and other private organizations.
I should like at this time to endeavour to define small business in the way in which we consider in the province from which I come and especially in the area which I represent. Small business is defined as one which would not be called upon to pay more than a corporation or private concern would pay on the first $25,000 of net profit, namely 20 to 25 per cent in income tax. That is a definition which I should like to advance concerning small business.
This government has made a promise and has taken steps to fulfil it. It has set up the machinery to answer queries and disseminate information concerning the incorporation of small businesses and their continuance. It has undertaken studies in the United States with the surprising result that here in Canada through the industrial development bank we loan on the ratio of 3 to 1 on capital compared with what is done in the United States on the basis of the same facilities as those available through the industrial development bank.
It is true that the industrial development bank does not answer the problem in full. It is limited in what it can do and those who suffer most are possibly those who are refused loans from that bank because they are in the retail or wholesale business. There is no doubt, however, that the powers of this bank could be extended so that its facilities could meet the problem of those who cannot qualify under the present restrictions.
The question of responsibility also arises. I should like at this moment to refer to the responsibility that rests with provincial jurisdictions. I speak of the province of Quebec which is very much concerned with small business. As a result of the action taken there, the corner grocery still exists in that province. Corner grocers are able to operate notwithstanding the competition of chain stores and the ensuing pressure confronting them. There are ways and means of making this possible. The province of Quebec has seen fit to allow the corner grocer to sell beer in his establishment and has denied that privilege to the chain stores.

There are various ways in which this government has already given aid to small business. I wish now to refer to those whom I consider the most underpaid people in the Canadian economy, the fishermen of the Atlantic coast. Every fisherman operates his own business, owning his own boat and gear. Through this medium he must provide a livelihood for his family. Through the years the federal government has provided facilities under which fishermen can borrow money. I refer to the loans made to fishermen at a rate of 5 per cent, of which they could take advantage if they wished. I refer to the assistance which has been given through the Fisheries Prices Support Act, fisheries salt assistance, the fishermen's indemnity plan, and research. These are some ways and means through which this government has come to the aid of small business. It is true that not enough has been done for the fishermen. Not long ago it was stated in this chamber that we must give to the western farmers a fair share of the national income. I am in favour of that, but let us not forget the eastern fishermen. They are also entitled to a fair share of the national income and we must find ways and means of ensuring this.
This government has instituted a special branch called the small business section in the Department of Trade and Commerce. I am quite confident that after this branch has studied the national problems of an economic nature, many of them peculiar to one region or unique because of geographic considerations, the government will find a way of meeting these problems through providing loans at a fair rate of interest.
We must remember that at this stage in the development of Canada when the rate of expansion is so greatly accelerated and when perhaps the funds normally available for this purpose are already being expended, to take action in this regard could bring about an increase in the rate of interest. But knowing the policies of this government, knowing that it is doing everything possible to hold down the rise in inflation and knowing that it is going forward steadily and intelligently, I am confident that very soon when the fury has subsided the government will implement some action which will make it possible for the small business sector of the Canadian economy to borrow money at reasonable rates of interest.

It was not
my intention to speak on this resolution today. I would much prefer to see it come to a vote and some decision taken by the house. However, after listening very closely to the debate, I have found that some very interesting things

Low Interest Loans to Small Business have happened. For one thing, we found out why nothing has been done by the present government in the last two or three years.
I know that most of the small businessmen were looking for big things after hearing all the glowing promises that were made in 1957 and in 1958. Unfortunately, since that time nobody has been able to define what a small business is, and therefore the present government has been unable to do anything about it.
One hon. member on the government side of the house mentioned the fact that while it is true we have not done too much for the small businessman, and there is not really very much we can do for them in regard to money because it is too hard to find, yet we shall give them plenty of advice and we may even improve on the advice we are giving to them.
When I was first elected to the House of Commons not too many small business people used to come to me to discuss their problems. They were far too well steeped in the good Tory propaganda that they must watch out for those socialists who were going to regiment them, and so forth. Therefore, for a long time none of the small businessmen saw fit to bring his problems to me. However, they were so busy watching the front door to see that socialists did not get in that they forgot to close the back door, and they found that their good free enterprising friends in the chain stores and corporations had been able to sneak in through the back door, sneak right up and catch them by the throat and strangle them.
One small businessman in my constituency came to me not very long ago. For many years he had been operating a small store. He had saved up all his life savings and he tried to enlarge his store and make it into a small supermarket. He wanted to know where all these stories had come from about money not being available. He said, "There is lots of money available. All you have to do is put a mortgage on your store, sign over all your life insurance, offer a discount here and there, and you will wind up paying 40 per cent." There is lots of money available. This is the biggest problem we have to face today. It is not a question of money not being available but just how much you are willing to pay for it. The money that a small businessman cannot get from the bank he can get from the finance company which gets it from the bank, I presume. I do not know where else you get it. But you have to pay three times, four times and five times the interest that is charged by the banks, and that money is always available, provided you are willing to pay usury rates for it.

If we had a little more work done on this problem and a little less talk about it, then we would have some hope of coming up with something to keep the small businessman in business in this country. If we do not, we shall find that the small businessman, like the family farmer, will pass out of existence.
I think it is time to get busy, do more work and have less talk so that we will have a vote on this resolution before ten o'clock tonight.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps all of us in the house this evening have noticed-and the hon. member who just took his seat drew attention to this fact-that there has been some difficulty this afternoon and tonight in defining big and small business. I should like to say that the debate this afternoon and this evening has pointed out to me that while there might be an intermediate course for bettering the situation that is facing small business and small businessmen, there are two courses that definitely can be followed in relation to the question. The first course, as we have learned from speaker after speaker, is not unlike the one that the United States adopted in 1953, when they set up a temporary small business agency which has since become an agency of a permanent nature. This also required a definition of small business.
However, for the lack of a better expression I may say there is the indirect effect that government policy could have in helping small business. It might have, as hon. members on the government side of this house have shown what you could almost term a direct effect in helping the small businessman in this country. It is this cumulative effect about which I want to talk. Time and time again we have made references to the small business section that has been established in the Department of Trade and Commerce. I would say that our approach to economic and business policy has been a wise one, not only
Low Interest Loans to Small Business for the large businessman but also for the small businessman. We have got away from that Howe attitude which resulted in the little man being forgotten for 22 years.
In giving thought, Mr. Speaker, to the part this cumulative effect has played, I want to make reference to the fact the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has made a great effort to cut down the non-statutory expenditures in our budget. This is helping in a very real way to reduce interest rates. When we are going in the direction of a balanced budget we are making a very real contribution toward holding the line on these rates.
I think it has to be said again and again to the Canadian people, and we should discuss it as hon. members in this house, that the government itself is a very large borrower. When the Minister of Finance takes such a reasonable course, this also is one of those things, I repeat, which helps with this general problem.
Another indirect policy, if you want to call it that, to which I should like to refer, is indicated in the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in relation to this proposition. I should like to say-

speechtext:
And you do not care what we do. For 22 years you did not care about the people of Canada, either, and you know where you are now. You are going to stay there a long time. You do not care about the little businessman, I know that. I recall in opposition days when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) would seek to give the impression of the bad Tories, the lackeys of St. James and Bay streets. Just the other day he said that we were attacking the big bad banks, and that is the old divide and rule game. The Liberals used to try to divide the big man from the little man. When we were in opposition we were the lackeys of Bay and St. James streets, and today we are attacking the big bad banks. A little consistency might be a good thing. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate used to join up with the former minister of finance to try to paint this picture, but it is not true today that the government does not care about the plight of the small businessman.
I should like to say that our party believes you cannot-although I am going to try to arrive at what some people might think is a definition later on-just draw a line between what you might call a big man and a little man as easily as all that. At the same time I do believe many speakers today have made reference to the fact that when the Prime
846	HOUSE OF
Low Interest Loans to Small Business Minister was speaking on television to the bankers of this country he was making a very real, honest policy plea to the banks. I think all of us who have been in small business or who have had anything to do with the small businessmen in our constituencies realize exactly what they are up against.
When the larger businessman is up against a problem, what happens? I visualize this type of situation. He is called in by the bank manager who says that there is a tough situation ahead so you had better broaden yourself out; we will give you a bigger loan limit, so to speak. The bigger businessman is forewarned of what you might call a credit pinch. However, the small businessman is not warned. When times get rough his credit is just cut off. He does not know where he is going. He finds he cannot get credit or the credit he has is cut off, whereas the bigger man is forewarned.
Oftentimes I suggest-I am subject to correction on this but it is something that I suspect-the larger businessman is not using up his full line of credit and yet the banks themselves call this extended credit. This makes it increasingly difficult for the little man to get credit which should be available to him. The banks should study this aspect of the problem.
I should like to draw an analogy for you. About three weeks ago I had the great pleasure of being invited to the Montreal forum to see a hockey game. You could not get tickets. There were thousands on the waiting list. As I went into the forum, I noticed there were box seats which were empty while the children in the poorer districts would have given their eyeteeth to see a hockey game. The boxes held by large corporations and the wealthy people were empty, while the people on the streets were desirous of seeing a hockey game and some of them perhaps never will see one. I say the same situation applies to credit. The larger corporations are not using up their full line of credit, yet the little man cannot get any. I am subject to correction on this, but this is a debating chamber and we are considering a problem. I believe cognizance should be taken of this fact.
There are no attacks on the banks here, Mr. Speaker. The policy of our government is simply to make sure that these financial institutions realize their stewardship involves more than making a profit. I should like also to join with other speakers in this debate in saying that I fully realize the industrial development bank, as it is currently set up, does not solve the problem we are discussing.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) tried to paint a black and white
[Mr. Grafftey.l

situation when he asked the question, are we for government subsidization on bank loans? While it might have been a good question to ask at the time, it has no bearing on this resolution. I point to the fact the resolution says, "by some means", so the question does not fall squarely within the motion.
At this point, I should like to offer what I feel might be a guide, a definition, of this very important problem. Again I come back to the question of a definition. I should like to say that others who have spoken in this house today have called attention to the United States experience and have said that you cannot superimpose the United States experience 100 per cent on our own national picture. In the United States the small business administration has a definition of small business which is as follows:
1.	A wholesaler, with annual sales of less than $5 million.
2.	A retailer (or a dealer in services), with annual volume less than $1 million.
3.	A construction company, whose annual receipts for the preceding three years have been less than $5 million.
4.	A manufacturer:
(a)	must have 250 or less employees:
(b)	manufacturers with between 250 and 1,000 employees are classed as small or large depending on their type of activity.
On the above basis, as was mentioned by another hon. member in this debate, 98 per cent of the United States companies are small businesses.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to some of the measures passed by the 85th congress. There were three important measures dealing with loans and tax relief for small business. The ceiling on the individual loans it may grant was raised from $250,000 to $350,000. This measure might not have too much bearing on our own particular situation here. The interest rate charged was reduced from 6 per cent to 5J per cent. Tax relief was also granted. It took the form of faster tax write-offs on new equipment in the first year after purchase; extension from two to three years of the period for which a loss may be carried back and applied against previous income to gain a retroactive tax refund. This next point is extremely important in relation to small family companies which often times are liquidated because of the difficulty in raising money for succession duty purposes. I refer to the provision made for 10 years instead of 15 months in which to pay estate taxes on a business held by a few persons.
The small business administration was set up in 1953 as a temporary agency to assist smaller concerns to obtain credit. Now it is a permanent independent federal agency

Funds will not go directly to the individual entrepreneurs but to certain qualified investment companies. Under the new law in the United States, the above-mentioned agency has been given $250 million in loan authority to furnish long term equity capital to small businesses.
I repeat that this whole matter in outline, as described in relation to the United States experience, cannot be superimposed on our picture. However, I thought that reference to it was pertinent at the present time.
Therefore in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me state simply that, in my opinion, while the government could possibly, like the United States, go into the direct loan field, backing certain loans for small business;- being a free enterpriser at heart I feel that the present government policy is a wise one. The matters that I have outlined-the cumulative effect of the policies we are now following-seem to me to be policies that recognize the problems of the small businessmen and small business and should be pursued to that end.
It is being stressed time and time again that the present administration is wisely following a policy of more goods produced by Canadians for Canadians in Canada. This certainly is encouraging our small businessmen. This certainly is encouraging what we might call our secondary industry and it is all part and parcel of the solution to the problem. The motion at present before the house calls for the provision of some means whereby low interest rates may be made available to small business. I should like to say that the members on the government side certainly have suggested and put on the record of this house many thoughtful suggestions, some of which might be taken up and added to what I repeat is the present wise government policy.
