speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I compliment the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) on his address here tonight and particularly for the assistance he has given the house with respect to the definition of what is small business. I think that is one of the problems that has been bothering all hon. members this afternoon and this evening. Certainly many have referred to the different definitions which commend themselves to different hon. members as to what in fact constitutes a small business. I think probably the difficulty hon. members find in making that definition is ample justification for the course that the government has been following in assembling information from the small businesses across the country, those who are interested in small business and the various organizations which have
Low Interest Loans to Small Business submitted briefs to the government on this matter containing opinions on what might constitute this particular classification of business. Obviously it is a difficult matter and is going to take a good deal of consideration and research before a final conclusion can be reached.
I was surprised this afternoon to hear interjected into this debate by the Liberals the allegation that this government has not moved rapidly enough in aid of the small businessman. Of course I welcome the fact that after 22 years the Liberals have discovered the small businessman. I am glad they have done so. I think all hon. members will welcome the opportunity that has been afforded for discussion of this important subject at this time in the house.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) mentioned the contribution the industrial development bank had made towards this problem. I think the observations he made in that regard were helpful. Certainly the industrial development bank has been of assistance to people in this country but obviously he must not be satisfied that the industrial development bank meets the need or else he would not have spoken in favour of this resolution.
I think all hon. members of this house will realize that much remains to be done in order to assist small businessmen in the difficulty they have in meeting the transformation of their businesses necessary to compete with the large enterprises which range across the country. I have seen many representations on this particular subject from individual retailers, from the retail merchants' association, from small manufacturers and from others. One particular contribution that I should like to mention at this time is a private research carried out by Mr. M. A. East, past president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, a small businessman in my home constituency and a person who has over the years devoted much time and attention to this particular problem.
I recall to hon. members the fact that the submissions of the retail merchants association of Canada, as set forth in a letter addressed to myself, included the proposition that the government should establish loan facilities through the chartered banks for small business to finance necessary capital expense and modernization to meet changing conditions. That is one of the facets of the problem which faces small business. To meet the general problem of small business there was contained in the speech from the throne of May 12, 1958 the following:
In order to assist small business, there will be established a small business section within the administrative machinery oi government. The functions of this organization will be to provide liaison

Low Interest Loans to Small Business
between government and small businesses, to study the problems of small business and to advise on measures necessary to meet them.
This small business branch has been established within the Department of Trade and Commerce. The staff has been employed. Investigations have been undertaken. Liaison has been effected with the United States and with the provinces in an effort to get at the problems which affect small businesses.
Everybody knows from first hand or from representations made by people in their constituencies the general problems affecting particular categories of small business. But the experience in the United States means that a good deal of investigation was necessary before the classification of these problems could be undertaken to a degree which might permit the government to take satisfactory action on them.
In this regard I would like to refer to something the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) said in this house, as reported in Hansard for July 16, 1959, at page 6140. He was outlining the terms of reference of the small business branch which was established by this government, and he said they were as follows:
1.	To act as a clearing house in referring inquiries of small business to the appropriate departments of the Canadian government or provincial or municipal governments and to various organizations and institutions;
2.	to compile and distribute bulletins and reports on topics of general interest to small business including information on government procurement;
3.	to assist small business on request to obtain statistical, technical and other information on management, production and marketing problems;
4.	to undertake studies concerning small business, particularly for guidance of the government in developing new policies in this field and as background material for dealing more effectively with the problems of small business;
5.	in the course of its work, to consult and co-operate with educational institutions, representative business associations and other private organizations.
As at July 16, 1959 the steps which had been taken by the government were outlined by the minister, and I think they should be set forth here in order that a clear understanding of what in fact has taken place may be brought to the attention of all hon. members. The hon. minister went on:
At the present time the branch has seven employees, including an assistant director and three research officers. The size of the staff has been kept small purposely during the initial stage of the branch's development until it is able to assemble information and make a report. The most important duties of the officers of the branch have been to advise on a program based upon the branch's terms of reference and the staff requirements for such a program. An important part of the work of the branch has been a review of studies relating to the problems of small business

in Canada and other countries and with the collection of quantitative and qualitative material on the position of small business in the Canadian economy.
You will notice from the two quotations I have just made, the emphasis I have placed on the direction of the government to the small business branch. They should undertake studies particularly for the guidance of government in developing new policies in this field; and to advise on a program based upon the branch's terms of reference and the staff requirements for such a program. Those are very necessary and very wise directives, because you just cannot develop small business assistance before you have the facts before you. The Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out in the same debate on page 6141 of Hansard:
-we have to have the facts. It is the assembling of the facts and information that is the duty and responsibility of the small business branch and the senior officials to whom the branch reports, who subsequently report to me.
Then he goes on:
I pointed out that in the United States financial aid to small business was only undertaken after years of investigation and experience in other bodies, and the same thing is going to be true in Canada. We have not said either yes or no with regard to this particular problem and are not going to give an answer one way or another until we have the facts before us.
The situation in the United States, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi was that long before 1953 the United States had been investigating this particular problem, and it was not until 1953 that they were able to establish even a temporary small business agency in order to carry out the initial work in this particular field. When the United States small business agency was authorized in 1958 to make provisions of small business investment companies expectations ran high. People in the United States thought that the program which had been developed up to that time in regard to loans made through the small business investment companies would be a real contribution to the solution of the problem. I would like to refer, if I may, to the feeling which was prevalent in the United States at that time. This is a quotation from Business Week of October 11, 1958:
This summer, congress tried to plug a wide gap in the nation's financial structure by authorizing a system of small business investment companies. Its purpose was simple: to extend to small businesses some of the same access to equity capital and long term financing that large business enjoys.
Suddenly, it's beginning to appear that congress opened up wider vistas than anyone had suspected. No one in Washington was prepared for the interest that has been shown-not only by small businessmen who hope for loans but also, and more significantly, by bankers and big investors. The Small Business Administration, which is still drawing up regulations with publication about three

weeks away, already has received well over 6,000 queries. At least half are concerned with investment possibilities.
Then under the heading "Wave of Excitement" the report goes on:
With this kind of interest on the investment-opportunity side, the system of S.B.A.'s begins to look like one of the most important changes in many years. One Washington official hails it as nothing less than another wave of enthusiasm like that for the mutual funds.
Before dealing with what in fact happened in the United States after their program had been inaugurated I should like to draw to the attention of the house just how this particular program was developed and worked. The S.B.A. had a revolving fund of $50 million to carry through to next June 30, with $200 million to be split between the next two fiscal years. This $250 million is only the seed for the system; the bulk of the capital for the S.B.I.'s will come from private sources.
Business Week, goes on to point out the following:
Emphasis is on the wide distribution of the financial help for small business. S.B.I.'s will doubtless be spotted geographically where the need is greatest and the alternate sources of financing are fewest. Moreover, they are not allowed to tie up more than 20 per cent of their paid-in capital and surplus in any one company they are helping.
Then they point out how they form a small business investment company:
An S.B.I. is a corporation set up by private organizers. They need a minimum of $300,000 in capital to start with, but up to $150,000 of this can be obtained from the Small Business Administration;
S.B.A. will buy debentures that are subordinated to all other paper except the common stock. There is no set time for redeeming these debentures, which will probably carry a 5 per cent interest rate.
To add to its original working capital, an S.B.I. can also borrow from S.B.A. up to 50 per cent of its paid-in capital and surplus, including whatever S.B.A. provided by buying debentures. A minimumsized S.B.I. thus could borrow another $150,000 at S.B.A.'s 5 per cent or perhaps 51 interest rate.
That was how the plan was to work. I just mention this because the summary of how the plan was to work indicates some of the problems which were faced before they could even contemplate setting up this form of assistance to small business. There was clearly a need to put this idea across and ensure a favourable reception for this project in the minds of the United States investors. The arrangement was that the S.B.A. would provide one part of the funds, and to that would be added the capital supplied by other investors. The S.B.I's have only one function: to provide the small business with long term funds, either through loans of up to 20 years, with a discretionary 10-year extension possible, or through purchase of debentures that are convertible into common
Low Interest Loans to Small Business stock at the creditor's option and at a sound market value fixed at the time the debentures are issued.
An S.B.I. can borrow and reinvest as much as four times its capital and surplus in contrast to regulated investment companies in the past whose borrowing has been limited to one third of their total assets. Thus, even the smallest S.B.I., with $150,000 in private capital matched by $150,000 from S.B.A., is empowered to line up $1.5 million for investment.
Then again, the S.B.A. set up a definition of small business to which reference has already been made. Perhaps it would be worth while to repeat it. The definition varies according to the industry concerned but generally the term covers retail and service businesses grossing up to $1 million a year, wholesale businesses grossing up to $5 million and manufacturing operations with up to 250 employees. In some industries the ceiling rises to 1,000.
That is an indication of the necessity for careful planning in this field and the considerations the S.B.A. had to take into account before developing the program which they put into effect. The result of the experience in the United States which, as I have said, was certainly hailed at its inception with great enthusiasm, is a result which we must all bear in mind when we are considering this resolution.
For a number of years the lending operations of this agency have been under criticism. The small business investment companies which were authorized under the small business investment act has been disappointingly small in number, and the field of operation has been restricted. It has been found that the loans made by these investment companies have had to be made at interest levels considerably above the general rate applied on similar loans to other borrowers. Once again the necessity for careful investigation is apparent to ensure that the small borrower is credit worthy and has a reasonable chance of utilizing the borrowed funds with success. These considerations have made the administrative cost of these loans very high. This has been the experience in the United States. As I say, the project was received with enthusiasm despite the intensive preparatory work which had been undertaken. The results have been disappointing.
This is no reason at all for us to say that this is something which should not be done. It is, however, reason for us to develop assistance to small businesses on a sound basis, on a basis which has been developed by contact with small businesses across the country and with those who have made a study of

Low Interest Loans to Small Business small businesses in order that our own small business branch may come to a sound determination of the policies which it recommends to the cabinet.
The diversity of problems encountered by small businessmen cannot be underestimated. The financial problem is not the sole problem; it is only one of the problems. Small businessmen must be assisted along a broad front-management, education, research, control of monopoly and the elimination of unfair competition are all subjects which must be dealt with, and are vitally important in our consideration of this particular matter. It is apparent from United States experience in this program of assistance to small business that the S.B.A. has been very conscious of the importance of management education.
As has been mentioned already this afternoon, it has conducted a widespread and worth-while educational program with seven different types of bulletin to provide information to the small businessman about the ways in which he can cut costs, the ways in which he can obtain markets, the ways in which he can improve his management, the ways in which he can start new businesses and about the ways in which small manufacturers as well as retailers may be assisted.
This program which is being developed by the government along these lines meets part of the problem. Hon. members will realize from what I have said that this small business branch which has been set up is intended not only to assist small businesses directly but also to assist them by providing advice to the government as to the best way in which small business can be helped. The S.B.A. in the United States has realized that the knowledge about the role and the importance of small business in the economy is very far from being complete. In consequence of this, last year the small business administration launched a research program. They have already been carrying on a program in which state agencies and educational institutions carry on projects to add to the knowledge of small businessmen. I suggest that all these steps are necessary in Canada.
The small business associations have been asking the government to assist them to obtain capital funds and in addition to attempting to realize improvements of good management practice they have asked the assistance of the government in promoting such good management practices.
I think all of us should become more fully aware of the important work that is being done in this area. In establishing the small business branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce this government has taken

a forward step of a type which will result in real assistance to the small businessmen of this country.
In the process of coming to grips with the whole problem of interested groups and individuals in this particular field, many have been making their views known to the government as well as to individual members of parliament. As I mentioned, I have received a number of briefs myself in which groups and individuals had set forth their views as to the way in which the government could be of assistance in this particular field. One such that I mentioned was a study carried out by Mr. M. A. East. In his letter of transmittal to me of his research brief dated October 20, 1958, he said:
It has become increasingly evident that the position of privately held companies in our Canadian economy is becoming rapidly less tenable respecting growth programming in relationship to that being developed by public companies.
I respectfully submit that the main reason for this condition resolves itself around the fact that privately held companies are restricted today in the matter of expansion programming because of capital account expenditure requirements and because of tax impact.
Canadian banks have done a good job over the years respecting the financing of inventories and accounts receivable for all forms of business, whether publicly owned or privately owned. Canadian bankers, nevertheless, with some exceptions, have not made long term capital account loans readily available to privately held companies. This situation has now reached a point where privately held companies cannot meet the capital costs of new machinery, equipment and plant that is required to match the expansion programming demanded of it. This situation, I believe, is especially true in the province of Saskatchewan.
Mr. East then goes on to point out some of the problems that small businesses are faced with in actual competition. He states:
May I draw to your attention a recent press release which indicated that a large steel fabricating plant is contemplated for establishment in Saskatchewan in 1959. The company in question is a public company. It has substantial holdings in Manitoba and Alberta, as well as in other parts of Canada; and now the economic pattern respecting the province of Saskatchewan has justified a capital account expenditure by this organization, which I understand will be very substantial.
By the word "our" in the next sentence, Mr. East refers to his own privately owned company. He went on to state:
Our privately held company is, therefore, faced with a condition whereby a large public company will be entering the Saskatchewan market because of the fact that an expanding Saskatchewan market exists which is not currently being adequately served by our own organization or others. It is, therefore, especially significant that our own privately held company is being placed in a noncompetitive position with a public company because of capital account. This condition has been developed during the past 10 years even though the profits of our organization have been in alignment with the national level and even though the net

earnings of the company have been largely plowed back into plant improvements and modernization by our company.
He then goes on to make a number of suggestions. I see that I shall not have time to go into his suggestions this evening. There is not sufficient time left at my disposal to embark on an adequate explanation of the solutions that he proposes other than to say that he feels there should be a source of long term borrowings through conventional sources such as banks, insurance companies and so forth that are able to provide this assistance for the benefit of privately held organizations.
He also makes reference to certain tax advantages which should be made available to small businesses in order that they may compete with large corporations on something approaching a fair basis. Large corporations are able to obtain finances by going into the public market with bonds and debentures, a course which small businesses certainly cannot follow. Small businesses have to depend for their capital at the present time on what they can borrow from the bank and on capital additions provided by friends or which can be plowed back from profits into their businesses.
I believe from what I have said this evening it has been amply demonstrated that the problem of small businesses is a very complex one. The problem of providing suitable assistance to them is one that must be solved in the light of the facts rather than upon a knowledge of partial facts. I believe that some form of capital assistance for small business particularly through the provision of funds at reasonable rates of interest would be most helpful but before this country embarks on such a course I should like to see analysed the reasons for the lack of interest in the United States in the small business investment companies which were so widely hailed at the time of their inception and which have apparently failed to do the job which the small business associations there set forth for them.
I believe it is evident that before this present resolution could be acted upon the house and the government should have brought before them not only the facts of the experience in the United States but also the facts of the Canadian situation which undoubtedly parallels in some degree the United States experience in terms of small business conditions.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege based on a Canadian Press report appearing
Question of Privilege
in this evening's Ottawa Citizen entitled, "Twenty Five Homes Raided in Toll Probe".
I should like to read three paragraphs from this article:
Montreal (CP)-The R.C.M.P. has launched a search for evidence of fraud or theft in toll collections on Montreal's Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges. They raided homes of 25 collectors during the weekend, it was learned today.
Superintendent R. J. Belec of the R.C.M.P. said papers and documents relating to income tax returns and property holdings were seized.
He did not elaborate and refused to comment on reports that previous investigations disclosed no evidence that could he used in court.
The R.C.M.P. began investigations two months ago after transport minister Hees said in Ottawa that revenues on the Jacques Cartier bridge increased sharply last summer after automatic toll collectors were installed. A parliamentary investigation into the toll collections is to begin in Ottawa this week.
You, sir, will recall that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) informed the house at the time he made his motion for an investigation into the tolls, and I quote from page 766 of Hansard:
There was no evidence that would support criminal charges.
He also assured the house that the moment any prima facie evidence is found against any person by that committee the investigation of that part of the case would be concluded.
It is true that the committee has not yet begun its investigation, and therefore the committee has found no evidence; but the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which the minister told us had not found any evidence up until the time he made his motion, is now reported to be collecting evidence and to have seized papers and documents.
My question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, which affects every hon. member in this house is that any investigation by a committee of this house should be suspended until the police investigation is completed and the law has taken its course; otherwise there will be two parallel investigations, and the investigation by the committee of this house might well deprive those involved of their right to a fair trial.
I feel sure that if the Minister of Transport had known that a further police investigation is under way he would not have made his motion as he did on Friday. I am sure he will be as anxious as we are to see that parliament does nothing to interfere with the course of justice. Therefore, I submit respectfully, that the investigation by the committee of this house should be suspended, and that the government should give consideration, if the police investigation warrants it, to proceeding instead with a judicial inquiry.
In fairness to myself I think I should add that I have made every effort to get in touch

Question of Privilege
with both the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) because of the statement which I have made; I have not succeeded and I am sure that both are detained because of other business.

Mr. Speaker, I entertain some doubts as to whether this is a proper question of privilege. I doubt the wisdom of entering upon this alleged question of privilege at five minutes before the closing hour today, when it might more properly be raised at the next sitting of the house, and particularly so when the minister of the crown who might wish to make a statement on this particular case is not present.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) has indicated that he made an effort to locate the Minister of Transport, who happens to be out of town on this occasion, and yet he has persisted in pursuing this question of privilege in the minister's absence.
The complaint that is being made by the hon. member for Laurier relates directly to the proposed investigation which was indicated to the house by the Minister of Transport, and I think that that minister should have been here before this matter was raised and certainly should be here before any conclusion is reached with regard to it. I note in Beauchesne's "Parliamentary Rules and Forms", fourth edition, 1958 at page 96, citation 105(3), the following:
A matter of privilege must be one which has recently arisen involving the privileges of the house, and calling for its immediate interposition.
I doubt very much whether the house needs to interpose itself at five minutes to ten o'clock on Monday night with regard to an investigation which has really not been entered upon by the House of Commons, although the ground work has been laid through the appointment of a committee.
The question of privilege is founded on a report which has appeared in one of the Ottawa papers. Whether that report is accurate or not the house is not in a position to discover at this moment, and I presume we would need to have the Minister of Justice here to confirm or deny the fact that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had been conducting the investigation alleged to have been made in the newspaper report.
I notice in Sir T. Erskine May's "Parliamentary Practice", 14th edition, at page 140 that when complaints are raised against members-and in effect this is a complaint against hon. members of this house-the comment is as follows:
Before making a complaint against a member it is the practice, as a matter of courtesy, to give him notice beforehand.
[Mr. Chevrier.l
If a member who makes a complaint against another member has failed or been unable to give the member notice of his intention to do so, or if although the latter has been given notice he neglects to attend, the more regular course is to adjourn further consideration of the matter of the complaint to a future day and to order the member whose conduct is impugned to attend the house in his place on that day.
I am not suggesting that the honour of any hon. member is being impugned on this occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  REFERENCE TO REPORT IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
I do suggest that without the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Justice present this matter of privilege should not be proceeded with because, as these comments go on to explain:
Where the member complained of is present when the complaint is made-
And this complaint refers to actions taken or contemplated by members of this house- *-it is the rule that he should be heard in explanation or exculpation as soon as the question on the motion founded upon the complaint is proposed from the chair-
And so on. I submit that in this particular instance that if there is no motion supporting this question of privilege there is nothing that the house can consider as being before it at this present moment, and I suggest that the matter be deferred. If the hon. member for Laurier wishes to raise it at the next sitting of the house, when the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Justice will likely be present, that will be the most suitable occasion to bring the matter to our attention.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  REFERENCE TO REPORT IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
May I be allowed to say a word in reply to what was said by the leader of the house who raised the point that first there was no question of privilege. I should like to draw to Your Honour's attention the fact that the matter could not have been raised earlier than it was because the committee sits tomorrow morning at ten o'clock. It will, therefore, not be possible to raise the matter when the house meets tomorrow afternoon at 2.30 o'clock. It will then have been too late; the committee will then have been seized of and entered upon the investigation. Therefore, this was the only time available following the report which appeared in the afternoon Citizen, and this was brought to my attention about six o'clock tonight. It was, therefore, not possible for me to raise it earlier than I did.
With reference to the other matter, I am afraid the leader of the house has entirely misinterpreted my suggestion. I have made no complaint. I have raised a question of

privilege and I have brought it to the attention of the house and the government in that, it seems to me, it would be entirely irregular to have two investigations being carried on at the same time; otherwise, there will be grave prejudice done to those who may afterwards be charged with criminal offences. I am simply bringing it to the attention of the government so that between now and ten o'clock tomorrow morning they will have an opportunity to consider the question of privilege I raise.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  REFERENCE TO REPORT IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Before anyone speaks further I want to assure myself that I understand the point raised by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). He complains that it would not be proper for the committee to proceed with this investigation in view of some act, some investigation or action of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police which has intervened since the house referred this matter to the committee. It seems to me this is more a matter relating to the proceedings of the house than a matter of privilege. I do not believe the hon. member asks for a statement that the committee is incompetent to proceed. It may be inadvisable for the committee to proceed if the subject matter before it should also be before the courts by way of a criminal charge. I do not believe the committee would proceed under those circumstances. The house itself usually observes the proprieties by refusing to discuss matters which are before the courts.
I think, perhaps, the hon. member by raising his point has done all he can do. I do not understand that he is proposing any motion. Do the two gentlemen who are rising desire to speak?

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  REFERENCE TO REPORT IN OTTAWA
speechtext: With all due respect to the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), first of all I would submit to you these representations are made on the basis of an unsubstantiated newspaper report. Second, the fact that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police may have commenced an investigation does not tell us the nature of the evidence that may be disclosed. There may be no evidence at all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  REFERENCE TO REPORT IN OTTAWA
speechtext: That is not what the report says.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  REFERENCE TO REPORT IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
There is nothing disclosed in the report as to the nature of the evidence. Unless the hon. member for Laurier is reading into the newspaper report the fact that there will be conclusive evidence on which a charge or charges may be based, then I do not see that he has a point. There are no charges laid nor are any in contemplation. Therefore, how could there possibly be a question of the privileges and rights of this house? I fail to
Business of the House see, with all due respect, how this point is properly taken at this time.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  REFERENCE TO REPORT IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
I want to agree with the substance of the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). I think it would be most inappropriate for a committee of this house to proceed with an investigation that is being paralleled by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Their investigation may lead to a court action which could be prejudiced by the investigation of a committee of this house. I am quite confident in my own mind that the members of the government would not approve of a committee of this house undertaking that kind of an investigation.
In so far as action from here on is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I would think that this is a question to be decided by the committee; that the committee itself has the power to make whatever investigation it feels is within its terms of reference. I would think that the members of the committee, tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock might very carefully examine the question of privilege that has been raised in this house, and should be most cautious in any investigation that they may undertake in order that the rights and privileges of citizens in this country may not be infringed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  REFERENCE TO REPORT IN OTTAWA
speechtext: I think the matter has been sufficiently discussed now that hon. members will know how to proceed from this point forward. In my opinion this is not a question of the privileges of the house, it is a question of the propriety of a committee proceeding, and the propriety of its proceeding tomorrow can be raised in the committee. If there are circumstances which make it improper for the committee to proceed, for example in the face of a pending decision of the courts, that would be a relevant matter to be raised then. I do not think there is a prima facie question of privilege of the house. It is rather a question of the privileges of persons outside the house.

PENAL INSTITUTIONS-PRE-RELEASE SYSTEM
speechtext:
1.	How many inmates of penal institutions under the authority of the federal government, by institution, have been released pursuant to the prerelease or gradual release system?
2.	What has been the experience of this system insofar as reformation, rehabilitation and recidivism are concerned?
Answer by: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of
Justice):
1.	During the years 1955 to 1959 inclusive there were 132 inmates of penal institutions under the authority of the federal government released pursuant to the pre-release or gradual release system. There were from Dorchester penitentiary, 7; St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, 10; Federal training centre, 2; Kingston penitentiary, 28 (male), 41 (female); Joyceville institution, 1; Collin's Bay penitentiary, 2; Manitoba penitentiary, 20; Saskatchewan penitentiary, 3; British Columbia penitentiary, 18.
2.	The general purpose of such a system or program prior to the release of an inmate on parole or at the expiry of his sentence is, especially in the case of longer sentences, to help him gradually readjust to community life and, in all cases, to assist him complete his post-release plans.
It is not possible at this experimental stage of this program to say much more than that immediate benefits have been realized where inmates have been enabled to obtain employment, pursue trades and education training programs, renew relationships with family.
The total answer may be known later from a pilot study which is now under way in the national parole service.
